question: A nurse wants to study past unconscious ICU dreams, but no records exist. Which research requirement is missing?

options.A: Clinical significance
options.B: Availability of data
options.C: Ethical clearance
options.D: Personal interest

explanation: If the information you need doesn't exist or can't be gathered, you won't be able to carry out that specific study. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T4#GNS217_U3_T4_h7)

question: What is the main goal of doing a literature review in nursing research?

options.A: To test a brand-new surgical instrument in the theatre
options.B: To collect brand-new blood samples from hospital patients
options.C: To interview hospital administrators about staff salaries
options.D: To summarize existing knowledge on a specific topic

explanation: Before starting something new, a literature review helps you check what is already known about a clinical issue by looking at past research. You've got this! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why do nurse researchers read past studies before starting a new project?

options.A: To guarantee that the new study will cost no money
options.B: To ensure that all previous researchers were entirely wrong
options.C: To bypass the need for any formal hospital ethical approval
options.D: To avoid repeating work that has already been done

explanation: Checking existing studies saves you time and resources so you don't reinvent the wheel on questions already answered. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h1)

question: When reviewing literature, what do we call the missing or weakly studied areas in current research?

options.A: Financial grants
options.B: Research gaps
options.C: Patient registries
options.D: Nursing licenses

explanation: Spotting what is missing in current studies points directly to research gaps that need investigation. Great job thinking like a researcher! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h2)

question: How does a literature review directly help with everyday bedside nursing care?

options.A: By lowering the monthly purchase cost of hospital drugs
options.B: By providing evidence to update hospital clinical policies
options.C: By replacing the need for direct physical assessments
options.D: By shortening the standard length of a nursing shift

explanation: Good research gives us the scientific proof needed to update old hospital procedures into safe, evidence-based practices for our patients. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h2)

question: Which of these is a classic example of a primary source in nursing research?

options.A: A systematic review article written by an outside professor
options.B: A newspaper editorial commenting on a new health policy
options.C: A textbook chapter summarizing ten different research articles
options.D: An original research report written by the scientists who did the study

explanation: Primary sources are direct, firsthand accounts written straight by the actual researchers who performed the study. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h3)

question: Why should a nurse be careful about relying only on secondary sources?

options.A: Secondary sources are impossible to find in standard medical library databases
options.B: Secondary sources contain only raw, unanalyzed numbers with no explanation
options.C: Secondary sources are interpretations that may introduce bias or missummarize the original data
options.D: Secondary sources are always illegal to reference in academic nursing papers

explanation: Since secondary sources are written by someone else retelling the story, relying on them alone can pass along misunderstandings of the original findings. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h3)

question: What does using the word AND do when searching an online database?

options.A: To automatically translate articles into English
options.B: To narrow your search by combining different concepts
options.C: To completely eliminate irrelevant foreign languages
options.D: To broaden your search by adding similar synonyms

explanation: Using AND tells the database to fetch articles containing all your search terms, which helps trim down a long list of results. You've got this! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h4)

question: A nurse wants to search for articles mentioning either 'pain' or 'discomfort'. Which search word should be used?

options.A: NOT
options.B: AND
options.C: WITH
options.D: OR

explanation: The word OR tells the database to look for either term, helping you catch helpful synonyms and expand your search. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h4)

question: When evaluating the methodology of a study, what are you mainly checking?

options.A: Which hospital cafeteria the researchers used
options.B: How the study was designed and carried out
options.C: How much money the lead author was paid
options.D: What color the cover of the journal was

explanation: Looking at the methodology means checking the sample size, tools, and design to see if the research was done properly and reliably. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h5)

question: Why is clinical relevance so important when reviewing a research paper?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any statistical calculations in the paper
options.B: It proves whether the authors paid their publishing fees on time
options.C: A study can be methodologically sound yet completely useless for your specific patient group
options.D: It guarantees that the journal has a high academic impact factor

explanation: Even if a study is well-designed, we must check if its findings actually make sense and work safely for the specific patients we care for every day. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is the key difference between summarizing and synthesizing literature?

options.A: Grouping multiple studies together by themes and trends
options.B: Deleting any study that disagrees with your personal opinion
options.C: Copying abstracts word-for-word into your own paper
options.D: Listing every single article in strict chronological order

explanation: Synthesis means weaving different studies together around common themes, rather than just listing one summary after another. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h6)

question: Why is a literature review considered weak if it only lists article summaries one by one?

options.A: It fails to show how the studies connect, contradict, or answer the main research question
options.B: It takes too much time to format correctly in standard APA style
options.C: It violates international copyright laws regarding academic journals
options.D: It forces the reader to look up all the original articles themselves

explanation: A simple list lacks deep analysis. True synthesis connects different findings to show broader patterns in the science. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h6)

question: What is the best way to organize the body of a literature review?

options.A: By the alphabetical order of the authors' first names
options.B: By the physical weight of the textbooks referenced
options.C: By the exact length of each published journal article
options.D: By themes, trends, or logical subtopics

explanation: Structuring your paper by themes lets you easily compare what different authors say about the same specific subtopic. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h7)

question: Instead of using long, direct quotes from research articles, what is generally preferred?

options.A: Omitting the authors' names completely to save writing space
options.B: Rewriting the data with different numbers to make it sound better
options.C: Paraphrasing the authors' ideas in your own professional words
options.D: Translating the quotes into a different language for variety

explanation: Paraphrasing shows you truly understand the concepts and helps your paper flow smoothly. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h7)

question: What do we call using someone else's ideas or words without giving them proper credit?

options.A: Synthesis
options.B: Plagiarism
options.C: Citation
options.D: Paraphrasing

explanation: Plagiarism means taking another person's work or ideas and presenting them as your own without acknowledging them. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a valid reason for providing proper citations in a literature review?

options.A: To avoid academic dishonesty and professional plagiarism charges
options.B: To give proper intellectual credit to the original researchers
options.C: To allow readers to verify the accuracy of your clinical claims
options.D: To make your reference list look as long and intimidating as possible

explanation: We use citations to give credit and let others check our facts—never just to pad the length of our bibliography! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T5#GNS217_U3_T5_h8)

question: When doing nursing research, what are the three main levels used to group literature sources?

options.A: Primary, secondary, and tertiary sources
options.B: Published, unpublished, and grey sources
options.C: Clinical, historical, and theoretical sources
options.D: Qualitative, quantitative, and mixed sources

explanation: You've got this! We group literature into three tiers based on how close the information is to the original study. Primary, secondary, and tertiary keep our research organized. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why do nurse researchers need to know the different tiers of literature sources?

options.A: To ensure that every single source used is an unpublished thesis
options.B: To guarantee that only historical textbooks are cited in the study
options.C: To eliminate the need for peer-reviewed journal articles entirely
options.D: To build a strong argument and avoid weak or biased data

explanation: Spot on! Knowing your source tiers helps you pick reliable evidence to back up your nursing care and assignments. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h1)

question: What makes a piece of writing a primary literature source?

options.A: It is a textbook summary written years after the original event occurred
options.B: It is an encyclopedia entry explaining general nursing theories
options.C: It is a library catalog used to locate published journal articles
options.D: It is a first-hand account written by the researchers who conducted the study

explanation: Brilliant! Primary sources give you the raw, direct data and methods straight from the team that did the actual study. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h2)

question: Which of these is a classic example of a primary literature source?

options.A: A dictionary definition of the medical term hypertension
options.B: A systematic review article analyzing the findings of fifty different research papers
options.C: A nursing pharmacology textbook chapter listing common drug side effects
options.D: A research report detailing the exact methods and statistical results of a clinical trial

explanation: You nailed it. A direct research report with its own methods and data is always a primary source. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h2)

question: What is the main job of a secondary literature source?

options.A: To list library call numbers for nursing textbooks
options.B: To collect brand-new raw data directly from hospital patients
options.C: To summarize, analyze, or synthesize findings from multiple primary studies
options.D: To provide a simple dictionary definition of medical terminology

explanation: Great job! Secondary sources do the heavy lifting of gathering and summarizing several primary studies into one readable article. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which secondary source uses math and statistics to combine the results of many different studies?

options.A: Primary clinical trial
options.B: Narrative textbook chapter
options.C: Meta-analysis
options.D: Case study

explanation: Awesome! A meta-analysis pools numbers from several studies together to give us a powerful big-picture answer. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which of the following is a normal example of a tertiary literature source?

options.A: A standard nursing pharmacology textbook
options.B: A randomized controlled clinical trial
options.C: A qualitative interview study with cancer patients
options.D: A systematic review of wound care methods

explanation: Spot on! Textbooks, handbooks, and encyclopedias are tertiary sources because they compile general knowledge for easy learning. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h4)

question: What is the main downside of relying only on tertiary sources like textbooks for brand-new clinical questions?

options.A: They focus exclusively on qualitative patient interviews
options.B: They contain too much raw, unanalyzed patient data
options.C: They can lag behind the most recent primary research findings
options.D: They are always written by anonymous authors without credentials

explanation: Correct! Because textbooks take time to write and print, they might miss the absolute newest discoveries happening in the hospital wards right now. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h4)

question: What actually happens during the peer-review process before a study gets published in a journal?

options.A: The government checking the document for tax and financial compliance
options.B: Independent experts in the same field scrutinizing the manuscript for quality
options.C: The journal editor publishing the manuscript without any changes
options.D: Patients voting on whether they liked the treatment described

explanation: You got it! Other experts in the field carefully review the paper to make sure the science is solid before the public reads it. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h5)

question: Which of these is considered a form of 'grey literature' in nursing?

options.A: A systematic review published in a commercial medical database
options.B: A policy report published by a government health ministry
options.C: A randomized trial printed in an international surgery journal
options.D: An article from a well-known peer-reviewed nursing research journal

explanation: Nice one! Government reports and conference papers published outside of standard commercial journals are known as grey literature. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h5)

question: Which online database is built specifically for nursing and allied health literature?

options.A: Lexicomp
options.B: Wikipedia
options.C: Google Drive
options.D: CINAHL

explanation: Spot on! CINAHL is every nursing student's best friend for finding trusted nursing journals and research. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h6)

question: Why do we use Boolean words like AND and OR when searching research databases?

options.A: To automatically translate foreign language articles into English
options.B: To convert secondary research summaries into primary data tables
options.C: To check if the author of a research paper has a valid license
options.D: To narrow or broaden search results to find relevant articles

explanation: Great work! Words like AND and OR help you filter your search so you don't get drowned in millions of unrelated papers. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h6)

question: What do we call sketchy publishers that charge money to print articles quickly without doing real peer review?

options.A: Predatory journals
options.B: Grey literature
options.C: Primary sources
options.D: Systematic databases

explanation: You're doing great! Predatory journals take cash from authors just to publish fake or unvetted work—always watch out for them! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h7)

question: Why is it super important to check the publication date of an article before using it for clinical care?

options.A: Patients refuse to answer questions about outdated medical research
options.B: Publishers charge higher fees for journals printed in the current year
options.C: Clinical guidelines and best practices change rapidly as new research emerges
options.D: Older articles are always written by students rather than doctors

explanation: Spot on! Healthcare changes fast. Using old research might mean you are practicing outdated, unsafe nursing care. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T6#GNS217_U3_T6_h7)

question: Why do we reference sources in nursing writing?

options.A: To acknowledge original authors and show evidence
options.B: To fill up empty space at the end of a paper
options.C: To make the essay or report look much longer
options.D: To prove that the writer memorized the textbook

explanation: You're doing great! Giving credit where it's due shows that your nursing points are backed by solid facts. Keep it up! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why shouldn't you rely purely on personal opinion in a nursing paper?

options.A: Instructors simply do not like reading personal thoughts
options.B: Clinical claims must rest on verifiable evidence
options.C: Personal opinions are always grammatically incorrect
options.D: It takes too much time to write out opinions

explanation: Spot on! Nursing is an evidence-based field, meaning we always back our care with proven facts rather than just guesswork. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h1)

question: What does plagiarism mean?

options.A: Forgetting to write a conclusion for your essay
options.B: Failing to use correct punctuation in a sentence
options.C: Passing off someone else's work as your own
options.D: Using a medical dictionary to look up a new word

explanation: Well done! Plagiarism is simply taking someone else's words or ideas and pretending they are yours. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h2)

question: If you accidentally plagiarize because you were rushing, how do schools usually treat it?

options.A: It carries severe academic penalties just like intentional cheating
options.B: It is excused automatically by university examination boards
options.C: It only counts if the student copied the exact title
options.D: It is completely acceptable as long as nobody notices

explanation: Good to know! Universities check for the final result, so always take your time to cite properly even when rushing. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h2)

question: Where do in-text citations usually go in a nursing paper?

options.A: At the very bottom of the page as small footnotes
options.B: Inside a separate appendix at the back of the book
options.C: Inside the body paragraphs near the borrowed information
options.D: Only on the title page beneath the student name

explanation: You've got this! In-text citations sit right inside your paragraphs to point readers to your sources instantly. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h3)

question: What is the main difference between an in-text citation and a reference list?

options.A: An in-text citation goes at the very end, while the reference list goes at the beginning
options.B: An in-text citation uses numbers only, while the reference list uses only author names
options.C: An in-text citation is brief, while a reference list entry gives full publication details
options.D: An in-text citation is optional, while the reference list is mandatory

explanation: Exactly! The short in-text citation gives a quick peek, while the reference list gives the full picture of the source. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h3)

question: Which referencing style is most commonly used in nursing and social sciences?

options.A: Chicago style
options.B: Bluebook style
options.C: OSCOLA style
options.D: APA style

explanation: Brilliant! APA format is a nursing student's best friend throughout school. You'll see it everywhere! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h4)

question: A medical journal uses little numbers in the text that match a numbered list at the end. Which style is this?

options.A: Harvard style
options.B: Chicago style
options.C: APA style
options.D: Vancouver style

explanation: Correct! Vancouver style uses numbers in the text to point straight to the numbered sources at the back. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h4)

question: What extra detail must you add when quoting an author's exact words in APA format?

options.A: The total word count
options.B: The publisher's city
options.C: The specific page number
options.D: The author's academic degree

explanation: You're doing awesome! Adding the page number helps anyone reading your work find the exact quote easily. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h5)

question: How are sources arranged in an APA reference list?

options.A: Chronologically from oldest publication year to newest
options.B: Alphabetically by the first author's last name
options.C: Numerically in the order they appeared in the text
options.D: By the length of the journal article title

explanation: Spot on! Arranging them from A to Z by the author's last name makes finding sources super easy. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h5)

question: What is the main job of reference apps like Zotero or Mendeley?

options.A: To write entire nursing essays and research papers
options.B: To block websites that contain plagiarized text
options.C: To store sources and automatically generate citations
options.D: To check student assignments for spelling errors only

explanation: Nice one! These tools save you stress by keeping your sources organized and generating citations for you. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h6)

question: Why should you always double-check citations made automatically by software?

options.A: Software can only format references in Vancouver style
options.B: Professors automatically fail any paper that uses software
options.C: Computers cannot recognize books, only journal articles
options.D: Software can make errors if source metadata is formatted poorly

explanation: You're a star! Computers are helpful, but a quick human check ensures your references are 100% error-free. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T7#GNS217_U3_T7_h6)

question: What is the primary role of a research question in a study?

options.A: It gives the study a specific focus and direction.
options.B: It proves the hypothesis before data collection begins.
options.C: It replaces the need for a comprehensive literature review.
options.D: It lists all the statistical tests to be performed.

explanation: A focused research question guides the entire investigation and keeps data collection relevant to the study aims. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why must a broad nursing topic be narrowed down into a specific research question?

options.A: Patient consent cannot be obtained for broad subjects.
options.B: Journal editors only accept narrow clinical topics.
options.C: Broad topics prevent the use of quantitative methods.
options.D: Broad topics are too complex to be investigated practically.

explanation: Narrowing a topic ensures the study is manageable and can be executed within practical time and resource constraints. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h1)

question: Which characteristic is essential for a valid research question?

options.A: It must guarantee a statistically significant positive result.
options.B: It must focus exclusively on rare medical conditions.
options.C: It must require advanced laboratory equipment to study.
options.D: It must be answerable through empirical investigation.

explanation: A research question must be capable of being investigated using data collected from observation or experimentation. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h2)

question: What makes a research question lack clarity?

options.A: Specifying the exact data collection tool to be used.
options.B: Including the target population in the primary sentence.
options.C: Limiting the study to a single clinical setting.
options.D: Using vague terms without precise operational definitions.

explanation: Vague terms confuse readers and researchers about what is actually being measured or observed. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h2)

question: What does a descriptive research question aim to do?

options.A: Prove a direct cause-and-effect relationship.
options.B: Document the presence or frequency of a phenomenon.
options.C: Test the effectiveness of a new drug.
options.D: Compare two opposing nursing theories.

explanation: Descriptive questions focus on observing and describing what is happening without necessarily explaining why. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h3)

question: A nurse researcher wants to know if handwashing compliance changes after an educational workshop. What type of question is this?

options.A: Causal question
options.B: Descriptive question
options.C: Theoretical question
options.D: Historical question

explanation: Testing if an intervention like a workshop produces a change in an outcome indicates a causal relationship. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h3)

question: What does the 'I' stand for in the PICOT framework?

options.A: Indicator
options.B: Investigation
options.C: Intervention
options.D: Interaction

explanation: In PICOT, 'I' represents the specific treatment, exposure, or intervention being tested. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h4)

question: Why do nurse researchers use the FINER criteria?

options.A: To draft the final conclusion of the research report.
options.B: To select the best statistical software for data analysis.
options.C: To calculate the sample size needed for statistical power.
options.D: To evaluate the overall practicality and value of a study idea.

explanation: FINER helps determine early on if a research topic is worth pursuing based on feasibility, novelty, and ethics. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h4)

question: How do clinical challenges usually contribute to the research process?

options.A: They reveal gaps in current knowledge that need investigation.
options.B: They replace the need for ethical committee approval.
options.C: They provide immediate statistical analysis for the ward.
options.D: They guarantee funding for clinical trials.

explanation: Everyday clinical problems highlight where current nursing guidelines are lacking or ineffective. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h5)

question: A nurse notices that patients on the surgical ward frequently complain of delayed pain relief. What is the best initial step toward framing a research question?

options.A: Review current literature on postoperative pain management protocols.
options.B: Immediately change the prescribed medication dosages for all patients.
options.C: Write a research hypothesis without checking prior studies.
options.D: Discontinue the use of standard pain assessment scales.

explanation: Reviewing existing literature helps determine if the problem is already solved or what specific aspect requires study. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h5)

question: What is the primary function of a research objective?

options.A: To summarize the final conclusions after data collection.
options.B: To provide a broad background of the research topic.
options.C: To state the specific aims or goals of the study using action verbs.
options.D: To list the names of all participating patients.

explanation: Objectives break down the overarching research question into concrete, actionable steps. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h6)

question: How does a hypothesis differ from a research question?

options.A: A research question requires statistical testing, unlike a hypothesis.
options.B: A hypothesis is always written as an open-ended inquiry.
options.C: A research question is only used in qualitative studies.
options.D: A hypothesis makes a predicted statement about the outcome.

explanation: While a question asks what is happening, a hypothesis proposes an educated guess about the expected result. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h6)

question: Why are yes/no research questions discouraged in academic studies?

options.A: They can only be evaluated using qualitative methods.
options.B: They fail to provide enough depth for meaningful analysis.
options.C: They automatically violate ethical research guidelines.
options.D: They prevent the researcher from obtaining informed consent.

explanation: Yes/no questions restrict the scope of inquiry and prevent a thorough exploration of variables. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended practice when writing a research question?

options.A: Checking that the study is feasible within resource limits.
options.B: Ensuring the question is specific and clearly defined.
options.C: Phrasing the question to lead the reader toward a desired outcome.
options.D: Framing the inquiry to address a genuine knowledge gap.

explanation: Leading questions introduce bias and compromise the objectivity of the research process. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T8#GNS217_U3_T8_h7)

question: What is the main job of research objectives in a nursing study?

options.A: To prove the researcher's personal opinions
options.B: To replace the need for a literature review
options.C: To state what the study aims to achieve
options.D: To summarize the final conclusions of the study

explanation: Think of research objectives as your study's compass! They simply spell out what you intend to find out so your project stays on track. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h1)

question: Why is it risky for a nursing research project to lack clear objectives?

options.A: The study will easily lose direction and gather irrelevant data
options.B: The nursing staff will refuse to participate in the study
options.C: The sample size will become too large to calculate
options.D: The hospital ethics committee will automatically grant funding

explanation: Without clear targets, you might end up collecting a mountain of unnecessary information that doesn't actually solve your clinical problem. Good objectives keep you focused! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h1)

question: How do research objectives help shape the design of a nursing study?

options.A: They dictate the exact salary of the research nurses involved
options.B: They automatically write the discussion chapter of the thesis
options.C: They determine whether you need a descriptive, survey, or experimental design
options.D: They dictate which hospital ward has the best ventilation

explanation: Your goal dictates your tools! What you want to achieve tells you whether you need to run a survey, observe patients, or set up an experiment. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h2)

question: Why do ethics committees carefully review a study's research objectives?

options.A: To decide which nursing journal will publish the final paper
options.B: To judge if the study poses any risks to participating patients
options.C: To calculate the total financial profit of the hospital
options.D: To verify the spelling and grammar of the title page

explanation: Ethics committees check your goals to ensure that whatever you plan to study is important enough to justify any potential burden on human participants. Patient safety always comes first! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h2)

question: What is the main difference in how a research objective and a research question are written?

options.A: A question uses medical jargon, while an objective uses everyday language
options.B: An objective is always a guess, while a question is a proven fact
options.C: An objective is written at the end of the study, while a question is written at the beginning
options.D: An objective is a declarative statement using an action verb, while a question is interrogative

explanation: Remember: an objective makes a statement using an action verb (like 'To determine...'), whereas a question asks something directly with a question mark at the end. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h3)

question: A nursing researcher states: 'To examine if handwashing frequency reduces hospital-acquired infections.' What is this statement?

options.A: A research objective
options.B: A data collection tool
options.C: A research hypothesis
options.D: A final study conclusion

explanation: Spotting an action verb like 'to examine' right at the beginning is a dead giveaway that you're looking at a research objective! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h3)

question: How many general objectives should a standard nursing research proposal have?

options.A: Only one
options.B: As many as the researcher wants
options.C: One for every chapter
options.D: At least five

explanation: Keep it focused! A study generally centers around one single overarching goal, meaning you only need one general objective. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h4)

question: What is the main job of specific objectives in a research study?

options.A: To list the names of all nurses participating in the study
options.B: To provide background history on the hospital ward
options.C: To break down the general objective into smaller, measurable tasks
options.D: To replace the need for a detailed literature review

explanation: Think of specific objectives as the baby steps that break your big main goal into manageable, actionable pieces. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h4)

question: In the SMART criteria for writing good objectives, what does the letter 'M' stand for?

options.A: Measurable
options.B: Methodological
options.C: Medical
options.D: Mandatory

explanation: The 'M' stands for Measurable. It ensures your objective includes clear indicators you can actually count, observe, or evaluate! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h5)

question: A nursing student writes this objective: 'To study everything about nurses.' Which SMART rule does this break the most?

options.A: Specific
options.B: Financial
options.C: Time-bound
options.D: Ethical

explanation: Saying 'everything about nurses' is way too broad! A good objective needs to be Specific so you know exactly what corner of nursing you are investigating. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h5)

question: Which of these action verbs should you avoid in a research objective because it is too vague?

options.A: To appreciate
options.B: To measure
options.C: To identify
options.D: To compare

explanation: Words like 'appreciate' or 'understand' are feelings—they are too subjective and impossible to measure accurately in a study. Stick to concrete verbs! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h6)

question: When setting up an experiment to test a new wound dressing, which action verb fits best in your objective?

options.A: To guess
options.B: To ignore
options.C: To compare
options.D: To admire

explanation: Since experiments look at how groups differ (like old dressing vs. new dressing), 'compare' or 'evaluate' are fantastic action verbs to use. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is a major trap to avoid when writing specific objectives for your nursing proposal?

options.A: Using action verbs at the beginning of every sentence
options.B: Ensuring the objectives are measurable and realistic
options.C: Aligning the objectives with the research methodology
options.D: Creating too many objectives that make the study lose focus

explanation: Having a laundry list of twenty specific objectives will scatter your energy and make data collection a nightmare. Keep your list tight and relevant! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h7)

question: Why is it discouraged to use the word 'prove' in a research objective?

options.A: It makes the study take much longer to complete
options.B: A single study gathers evidence to test a hypothesis, rather than proving an absolute truth
options.C: The word 'prove' is grammatically incorrect in scientific writing
options.D: Ethics committees do not allow researchers to have strong opinions

explanation: Science builds knowledge brick by brick. A single study only gathers evidence to support or reject an idea—it rarely claims to 'prove' an absolute truth once and for all. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h7)

question: In nursing research, what do we actually mean by 'measurement'?

options.A: Recording vital signs only during morning rounds
options.B: Assigning numbers or labels to objects or events
options.C: Prescribing medication according to hospital policy
options.D: Treating patients based on their personal preferences

explanation: Think of measurement simply as giving a number or a clear label to something we are observing, following a set of rules. You've got this! [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why is it important for a nurse researcher to know about different scales of measurement?

options.A: To calculate the exact financial cost of a hospital ward
options.B: To determine which nurses get promoted to head nurse
options.C: To bypass the hospital ethics committee approval process
options.D: To select the correct statistical tests for data analysis

explanation: Different types of data need different mathematical tools. Knowing your measurement scale helps you pick the right statistical test to make sense of your findings. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h1)

question: Which of these best describes a nominal scale of measurement?

options.A: Variables contain a true and absolute zero point
options.B: Data points are always ranked from highest to lowest
options.C: Measurements have equal intervals between numbers
options.D: Categories have no numerical value or logical order

explanation: Nominal data is just about naming or sorting into groups (like male/female or blood types). One group isn't higher or lower than another! [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h2)

question: Which of these clinical variables is measured using a nominal scale?

options.A: Weight of an infant in kilograms
options.B: Patient admission diagnosis code
options.C: Body temperature in degrees Celsius
options.D: Pain score rated from zero to ten

explanation: Diagnosis codes are just labels used to group patient conditions. A malaria code isn't 'higher' than a typhoid code—they're just different categories. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h2)

question: What is the main catch or limitation when using an ordinal measurement scale?

options.A: Categories cannot be placed in any logical sequence
options.B: The exact mathematical distance between ranks is unknown
options.C: It requires a true zero point to function correctly
options.D: It cannot be used for any kind of health research

explanation: Ordinal scales let us put things in order (like mild, moderate, severe), but they don't tell us if the gap between mild and moderate is the same as moderate and severe. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h3)

question: A nurse assesses a wound and notes it as 'mild, moderate, or severe'. What scale of measurement is this?

options.A: Ratio scale
options.B: Nominal scale
options.C: Interval scale
options.D: Ordinal scale

explanation: Because the wound grades follow a clear rank order from best to worst, we call this an ordinal scale. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h3)

question: What is the standout feature of an interval scale of measurement?

options.A: It contains categories that cannot be placed in any order
options.B: It possesses an absolute zero point representing total absence
options.C: It is used exclusively for measuring physical weight and mass
options.D: It has equal intervals between numbers but no true zero

explanation: On an interval scale, the steps between numbers are even (like degrees on a thermometer), but zero doesn't mean 'nothing'—0°C doesn't mean there is zero heat! [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h4)

question: Why is 30 degrees Celsius not considered twice as warm as 15 degrees Celsius?

options.A: Because Celsius measurements have uneven gaps between numbers
options.B: Because the scale lacks a true absolute zero point
options.C: Because thermal energy cannot be measured numerically
options.D: Because temperature is actually measured on a nominal scale

explanation: Without a true zero point where temperature completely disappears, you can't multiply or say something has 'twice as much' heat. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h4)

question: Which special property sets a ratio scale apart from an interval scale?

options.A: The presence of unequal intervals between numbers
options.B: The use of categories that cannot be ranked
options.C: The complete absence of any numerical values
options.D: The presence of an absolute true zero point

explanation: A true zero means zero actually means none of that item exists (like 0 mL of urine output). That's what makes it a ratio scale! [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h5)

question: A nurse records a patient's daily urine output as 1000 mL, which is exactly double yesterday's output. What scale makes this math possible?

options.A: Ratio scale
options.B: Interval scale
options.C: Ordinal scale
options.D: Nominal scale

explanation: Because urine output has a true zero (0 mL means absolutely no urine), you can safely make direct comparisons like 'twice as much'. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h5)

question: How do the four scales of measurement relate to one another?

options.A: Lower scales are more accurate than higher ratio scales
options.B: Nominal and ratio scales are identical except for their names
options.C: All four scales share the exact same mathematical properties
options.D: Higher scales build upon the rules of lower scales by adding features

explanation: Each scale keeps the perks of the previous one while adding a cool new mathematical power. Nominal is basic, ordinal adds rank, interval adds equal spacing, and ratio adds true zero! [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h6)

question: Which of the following measurement scales includes BOTH equal intervals and a true zero?

options.A: Ratio scale
options.B: Nominal scale
options.C: Interval scale
options.D: Ordinal scale

explanation: The ratio scale sits at the top of the ladder—it has both evenly spaced numbers and a real, absolute zero. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h6)

question: Why is it usually smart to collect data at the highest possible level of measurement?

options.A: Nominal scales require more complex computer software to analyze
options.B: Lower-level data is illegal to use in modern hospital research
options.C: Ratio scales prevent patients from refusing to answer survey questions
options.D: You can convert higher-level data down into categories later if needed

explanation: If you collect precise numbers, you can always group them later. But if you start with vague categories, you've lost the exact details forever! [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h7)

question: A nurse researcher wants to measure patient satisfaction in the most detailed way possible. Which option should they choose?

options.A: Asking patients to answer simply yes or no to being satisfied
options.B: Using a continuous numerical rating scale from zero to one hundred
options.C: Grouping patients into satisfied, neutral, or dissatisfied categories
options.D: Classifying hospital units by their primary nursing delivery model

explanation: A 0-100 rating gives you rich, detailed numbers instead of forcing patients into simple yes/no boxes. Great job working through these! [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary use of a line diagram in healthcare data?

options.A: Displaying static demographic categories
options.B: Comparing percentages of a whole population
options.C: Listing individual patient case histories
options.D: Showing changes in variables over time

explanation: Line diagrams connect data points to clearly display continuous trends over sequential periods like weeks or years. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h1)

question: Why do nurses prefer line graphs over data tables for showing trends?

options.A: They eliminate the need for statistics
options.B: They make patterns over time instantly visible
options.C: They prevent any form of misinterpretation
options.D: They require fewer data points to construct

explanation: Visual lines allow clinicians to spot trajectory changes much faster than scanning rows of numbers. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h1)

question: Which variable is normally plotted on the horizontal X-axis of a graph?

options.A: Patient count
options.B: Time interval
options.C: Percentage rate
options.D: Temperature value

explanation: The X-axis standardly holds the independent variable, which represents sequential progression like time. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h2)

question: What happens to a line graph when the axis scales are unevenly spaced?

options.A: Data points automatically realign
options.B: Trends become distorted and misleading
options.C: The independent variable shifts to the Y-axis
options.D: Statistical significance increases

explanation: Inconsistent scale intervals stretch or compress lines artificially, exaggerating or hiding real clinical changes. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h2)

question: A graph that displays both male and female recovery rates using separate lines on the same grid is called what?

options.A: Simple line graph
options.B: Component line graph
options.C: Multiple line graph
options.D: Univariate scatter plot

explanation: Multiple lines on shared axes allow direct comparison of two or more distinct groups over the same timeframe. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h3)

question: When should a nurse researcher choose a simple line graph?

options.A: When comparing multiple departments across various metrics
options.B: When dividing a single total sum into parts
options.C: When showing correlation without a time element
options.D: When tracking a single health indicator over time

explanation: A simple line graph focuses cleanly on one variable's progression without visual clutter from extra lines. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h3)

question: What important detail must be included alongside axis labels on a clinical graph?

options.A: Units of measurement
options.B: Statistical p-values
options.C: Patient registration numbers
options.D: The researcher's signature

explanation: Explicit units like milligrams or days prevent ambiguity regarding what the numbers represent. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h4)

question: A nurse is drawing a graph of hourly pulse rates. What should be done first?

options.A: Draw the connecting lines between distant points
options.B: Calculate the final percentage increase
options.C: Select a complex multi-colored design template
options.D: Organize the time and pulse data into a table

explanation: Data must be systematically organized before axes can be scaled and points plotted accurately. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h4)

question: What does a sharp upward slope on a hospital incident graph indicate?

options.A: An increase in the recorded variable over time
options.B: A decrease in overall departmental workload
options.C: A complete stabilization of patient admissions
options.D: An error in the initial data collection table

explanation: Upward trajectories signify that values on the vertical axis are growing larger as time progresses. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h5)

question: A line graph of ward typhoid cases shows a sudden spike during the rainy season. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.A: The graph axes were labeled incorrectly
options.B: Patient record-keeping has become entirely random
options.C: Environmental factors may be driving a temporary outbreak
options.D: Treatment protocols have successfully eradicated the disease

explanation: Sudden spikes in seasonal disease data typically point to real-world epidemiological shifts rather than graph errors. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h5)

question: Which of the following practices should be avoided when creating a line graph?

options.A: Adding a descriptive title that summarizes the data
options.B: Including a clear legend to explain different line types
options.C: Overcrowding the chart with too many overlapping lines
options.D: Starting the Y-axis at zero for standard measurements

explanation: Too many lines clutter the visual space and defeat the purpose of clear data presentation. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h6)

question: Why is cutting off the bottom of the Y-axis without a break mark considered bad practice?

options.A: It violates international research publishing laws
options.B: It prevents the X-axis from showing proper time intervals
options.C: It automatically deletes historical data points
options.D: It exaggerates minor data changes and misleads viewers

explanation: Cutting off the base of the Y-axis makes small differences look massive, creating false alarms in clinical data. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T10#GNS217_U4_T10_h6)

question: What does an ogive graph show in research data?

options.A: A categorical variable count
options.B: A cumulative frequency distribution
options.C: A simple mean value trend
options.D: A standard deviation spread

explanation: An ogive is a graph specifically designed to plot cumulative frequencies against class boundaries. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h1)

question: Why would a researcher use an ogive instead of a standard histogram?

options.A: To compare two completely unrelated patient diagnoses
options.B: To find the precise daily medication dosage errors
options.C: To see total observations falling above or below a value
options.D: To calculate the exact mode of a nominal data set

explanation: Cumulative graphs like ogives display running totals, making it easy to see how many data points accumulate past a certain point. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h1)

question: What is a running total of frequencies called in statistics?

options.A: Class midpoint
options.B: Relative frequency
options.C: Standard frequency
options.D: Cumulative frequency

explanation: Cumulative frequency continuously adds up the frequency values from one interval to the next. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of class boundaries when plotting an ogive?

options.A: To eliminate gaps between numerical data intervals
options.B: To determine the most common diagnosis in a ward
options.C: To increase the total number of patient records
options.D: To calculate the average age of the patients

explanation: Using exact class boundaries ensures the graph's horizontal axis is continuous without missing numerical values between bins. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h2)

question: Which direction does a 'less than' ogive slope on a graph?

options.A: Vertically straight up and down
options.B: Flat across the middle axis
options.C: Downward from left to right
options.D: Upward from left to right

explanation: A 'less than' ogive always rises because cumulative frequencies increase as you move toward higher values. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h3)

question: What does a 'greater than' ogive typically measure?

options.A: The lowest single recorded value in a study
options.B: The exact average of all patient wait times
options.C: Observations that exceed a specific lower boundary
options.D: Frequencies that decrease from left to right

explanation: Greater-than cumulative graphs track values that meet or exceed specific thresholds moving backward through the data. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h3)

question: What value starts the line on the horizontal axis of a 'less than' ogive?

options.A: The highest frequency in the data set
options.B: The median value of the entire study
options.C: The lower boundary of the first class
options.D: The total number of patients sampled

explanation: An ogive always begins on the X-axis at the lower boundary of the first class where cumulative frequency is zero. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h4)

question: When plotting an ogive, what data goes on the vertical Y-axis?

options.A: Raw individual scores
options.B: Class intervals
options.C: Midpoints of data
options.D: Cumulative frequencies

explanation: The vertical axis of any ogive represents the running total or cumulative frequency of the observations. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h4)

question: Which percentile matches the median on an ogive graph?

options.A: 100th percentile
options.B: 25th percentile
options.C: 75th percentile
options.D: 50th percentile

explanation: The median divides a data set in half, matching the 50 percent mark on the cumulative frequency axis. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h5)

question: How do you find the third quartile using a completed ogive graph?

options.A: Find the highest peak on the X-axis and divide it by two
options.B: Locate 75 percent on the Y-axis and read the matching X value
options.C: Locate 25 percent on the X-axis and look up to the curve
options.D: Measure the total height of the Y-axis and multiply by ten

explanation: The third quartile represents 75 percent of the cumulative data, found by matching the 75 percent mark on the Y-axis to the X-axis. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h5)

question: How can a nurse manager use an ogive in an emergency department?

options.A: To order medical supplies based on hospital branding
options.B: To calculate the exact salary of every nurse on duty
options.C: To determine what percentage of patients wait less than a specific time
options.D: To schedule the weekly holiday roster for ward staff

explanation: Ogives let managers easily read cumulative percentages, such as how many patients were seen under a target time limit. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h6)

question: A public health nurse wants to know how many children received immunizations below a target age. Which graph is best?

options.A: A simple bar graph
options.B: A basic scatter plot
options.C: A standard pie chart
options.D: A 'less than' ogive

explanation: A 'less than' ogive explicitly shows how many cumulative observations fall below a given upper boundary or target. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T11#GNS217_U4_T11_h6)

question: What type of data does a scatter diagram display?

options.A: Univariate data
options.B: Categorical data
options.C: Nominal data
options.D: Bivariate data

explanation: Scatter diagrams plot two continuous variables simultaneously to show their relationship, which defines bivariate data. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h1)

question: On which axis is the independent variable traditionally placed?

options.A: Diagonal axis
options.B: Horizontal axis
options.C: Vertical axis
options.D: Z-axis

explanation: The horizontal axis, or X-axis, conventionally holds the predictor or independent variable. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h1)

question: A primary benefit of using scatter diagrams in healthcare research is to...

options.A: Visually assess relationships between variables
options.B: Replace clinical judgement entirely
options.C: Diagnose individual patient pathologies
options.D: Calculate exact medication dosages

explanation: The main purpose of a scatter plot is to give researchers a visual display of how two variables interact. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h2)

question: A nurse manager plots ward staffing levels against medication errors on a scatter diagram to...

options.A: Calculate the hospital budget for nursing staff
options.B: Prove definitive legal liability for an incident
options.C: Explore potential connections between staffing and errors
options.D: Determine the exact shift schedule for next month

explanation: Scatter diagrams are used in quality improvement to explore possible relationships between operational metrics like staffing and clinical errors. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h2)

question: What does each individual dot on a scatter diagram represent?

options.A: A paired set of measurements for one subject
options.B: The average score of the entire study population
options.C: A calculated statistical error value
options.D: The total number of patients admitted in a day

explanation: Each point corresponds to the specific X and Y values recorded for a single observation or patient. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h3)

question: Uneven scaling on the axes of a scatter diagram will cause...

options.A: An increase in the total sample size
options.B: Distortion of the visual pattern of data points
options.C: Elimination of the independent variable
options.D: Automatic correction of statistical outliers

explanation: Poor or unequal scaling stretches or compresses the graph, making relationships look stronger or weaker than they actually are. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h3)

question: The very first step in constructing a scatter diagram is to...

options.A: Draw the vertical Y-axis and horizontal X-axis
options.B: Gather your paired bivariate data values
options.C: Calculate the final correlation coefficient
options.D: Add a descriptive title to the graph

explanation: You must first collect your paired observations before you can design axes or plot any data points. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h4)

question: Why must axes on a scatter diagram include units of measurement?

options.A: To ensure clarity and prevent clinical misinterpretation
options.B: To hide extreme data points from reviewers
options.C: To make the graph fit standard printer paper
options.D: To satisfy software licensing requirements

explanation: Clear labels and units prevent anyone reading the chart from misinterpreting the scale or meaning of the variables. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h4)

question: A scatter plot where dots trend downward from left to right shows a...

options.A: Negative correlation
options.B: Zero correlation
options.C: Positive correlation
options.D: Perfect correlation

explanation: A downward slope means that as one variable goes up, the other goes down, which defines a negative correlation. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h5)

question: What does a tight, narrow cluster of dots along a straight line indicate?

options.A: A negative clinical outcome for patients
options.B: A strong correlation between the variables
options.C: An error in recording the independent variable
options.D: A complete absence of data points

explanation: The closer data points cluster to an imaginary line, the stronger the relationship between the two variables. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h5)

question: What is an outlier on a scatter diagram?

options.A: The highest value recorded on the vertical axis
options.B: The exact center point where the axes cross
options.C: A data point lying far away from the main cluster
options.D: A line drawn through the middle of the data

explanation: Outliers are isolated points that do not follow the general trend of the rest of the dataset. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h6)

question: How should a researcher initially handle an unexpected outlier in clinical data?

options.A: Investigate the point for measurement or entry errors
options.B: Change the scale of the graph to hide it
options.C: Ignore it completely without checking the patient file
options.D: Immediately delete it to improve the graph's appearance

explanation: Outliers require investigation to determine if they are genuine clinical variations or simple mistakes before deciding how to handle them. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h6)

question: Why is it incorrect to assume causation from a strong scatter diagram correlation?

options.A: Data points are always randomly generated
options.B: Confounding factors may influence both variables
options.C: Scatter diagrams only display categorical data
options.D: The horizontal axis cannot represent time

explanation: Correlation shows an association, but external or confounding variables may be responsible for the observed pattern rather than direct cause and effect. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h7)

question: A study shows a scatter plot with a positive correlation between patient age and blood pressure. What does this visualization actually demonstrate?

options.A: Older age is associated with higher blood pressure in this sample
options.B: Aging is the direct physiological cause of hypertension in every patient
options.C: Blood pressure causes patients to age at a faster rate
options.D: The blood pressure cuff used in the study was malfunctioning

explanation: Scatter diagrams demonstrate association or correlation between variables, not definitive physiological causation. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T12#GNS217_U4_T12_h7)

question: Which type of data is best analyzed using a Chi-Square test?

options.A: Normally distributed averages
options.B: Categorical data
options.C: Ratio level measurements
options.D: Continuous numerical data

explanation: Chi-Square tests evaluate frequencies and counts within discrete groups rather than continuous numerical values. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h1)

question: Why would a nurse researcher choose a non-parametric test like Chi-Square?

options.A: To prove cause and effect in clinical trials
options.B: To analyze data measured in categories or frequencies
options.C: To measure blood pressure changes over time
options.D: To calculate the exact mean and standard deviation

explanation: Categorical variables such as infection status or marital status require non-parametric methods like Chi-Square because they lack continuous numerical properties. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h1)

question: What is the minimum recommended expected frequency for each cell in a Chi-Square table?

options.A: At least 10
options.B: At least 5
options.C: At least 20
options.D: At least 50

explanation: Cells with very low expected counts undermine the mathematical stability of the Chi-Square distribution. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h2)

question: A clinical researcher measures the same patients before and after an intervention using a Chi-Square test. Which basic assumption is violated here?

options.A: Normal distribution
options.B: Equal variance
options.C: Independent observations
options.D: Random sampling

explanation: Measuring the same subject multiple times creates paired or dependent data, which violates the independence requirement of standard Chi-Square tests. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h2)

question: Which specific Chi-Square test evaluates the relationship between two categorical variables?

options.A: Goodness-of-fit test
options.B: Paired sample t-test
options.C: Test of independence
options.D: Pearson correlation test

explanation: The test of independence examines two variables simultaneously to see if they are associated or related. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h3)

question: A nurse wants to know if patient satisfaction ratings in a local clinic match national percentages. Which test should be used?

options.A: Linear regression
options.B: Goodness-of-fit test
options.C: ANOVA test
options.D: Test of independence

explanation: Comparing a single sample's categorical breakdown against a known standard or expected population proportion requires a goodness-of-fit test. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h3)

question: What does the null hypothesis typically state in a Chi-Square test of independence?

options.A: The expected frequencies are all equal to zero
options.B: The sample data is completely invalid
options.C: A strong causal relationship exists between variables
options.D: No association exists between the two variables

explanation: The null hypothesis always assumes independence or no relationship between the studied variables until proven otherwise. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h4)

question: What does rejecting the null hypothesis in a Chi-Square test suggest?

options.A: The data collection method was flawed
options.B: Causation between variables has been confirmed
options.C: An association likely exists between the variables
options.D: The sample size was too small to be useful

explanation: A significant Chi-Square result points to a statistical relationship, though it cannot establish cause and effect by itself. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h4)

question: What do observed frequencies represent in a Chi-Square calculation?

options.A: Actual data counts collected from the study
options.B: Theoretical values predicted by the null hypothesis
options.C: The total number of variables in the research
options.D: The level of significance chosen by the researcher

explanation: Observed frequencies are the real, empirical counts recorded from the participants during data collection. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h5)

question: How are expected frequencies calculated for a cell in a contingency table?

options.A: Observed frequency subtracted from the total sample size
options.B: Row total multiplied by column total, divided by grand total
options.C: Grand total multiplied by the significance level
options.D: Column total divided by the number of categories

explanation: The mathematical formula for expected cell frequency multiplies the corresponding row and column totals and divides by the overall sample size. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h5)

question: What standard alpha level is commonly used to determine statistical significance in nursing research?
explanation: A p-value threshold of 0.05 represents the standard benchmark for rejecting the null hypothesis in healthcare studies. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h6)

question: What does a high p-value greater than 0.05 indicate about study results?

options.A: The sample size was definitely too large
options.B: The null hypothesis must be rejected immediately
options.C: Observed patterns could easily occur by chance
options.D: A strong causal link has been discovered

explanation: A high p-value means there is not enough evidence to rule out random variation as the cause of the data pattern. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h6)

question: Which of the following elements is NOT required when reporting a Chi-Square test result?

options.A: The p-value
options.B: The test statistic value
options.C: The degrees of freedom
options.D: The exact blood pressure averages

explanation: Blood pressure averages are continuous measurements unrelated to reporting standard categorical Chi-Square test statistics. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h7)

question: A research paper reports a Chi-Square test result as χ²(1, N = 200) = 4.12, p = 0.04. What should the nurse researcher do?

options.A: Calculate the mean and median for the categorical groups
options.B: Discard the study because the sample size is inadequate
options.C: Reject the null hypothesis because the p-value is below 0.05
options.D: Accept the null hypothesis because the test statistic is low

explanation: Since 0.04 is less than the standard 0.05 threshold, the finding is statistically significant, warranting rejection of the null hypothesis. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T13#GNS217_U4_T13_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a t-test in nursing research?

options.A: To measure the incidence of chronic diseases
options.B: To compare means between two groups
options.C: To determine the sample size for a study
options.D: To calculate the percentage of patient survival

explanation: A t-test evaluates whether the average values of two specific groups differ significantly from each other. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h1)

question: Why do nurse researchers use inferential statistics like the t-test?

options.A: To summarize the basic demographics of the ward
options.B: To check if study results happened by chance
options.C: To replace the need for ethical committee approval
options.D: To list the qualitative feedback from patients

explanation: Inferential statistics help determine if an intervention caused a real difference rather than random variation. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h1)

question: The null hypothesis always assumes which of the following?

options.A: The alternative hypothesis is proven true
options.B: The sample size is too small to analyze
options.C: No difference exists between group means
options.D: A strong positive correlation is present

explanation: The null hypothesis acts as a baseline assumption that the intervention had no effect whatsoever. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h2)

question: A researcher states that a new wound dressing changes healing time. What type of hypothesis is this?

options.A: Null hypothesis
options.B: Descriptive hypothesis
options.C: Retrospective hypothesis
options.D: Alternative hypothesis

explanation: The alternative hypothesis proposes that a real relationship or difference exists due to the intervention. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h2)

question: What type of data scale is required for the dependent variable in a t-test?

options.A: Continuous scale
options.B: Nominal scale
options.C: Ordinal ranking
options.D: Categorical scale

explanation: The t-test requires continuous numerical data like blood pressure readings or body temperature. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h3)

question: Homogeneity of variance means which of the following about the groups?

options.A: Their spreads or variances are roughly equal
options.B: Their mean values must equal zero
options.C: Their distributions must be completely skewed
options.D: Their sample sizes must be identical

explanation: Homogeneity of variance ensures that the dispersion of data points is similar across the groups being compared. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h3)

question: Which test should a nurse use to compare blood pressure in the same patients before and after exercise?

options.A: Analysis of variance
options.B: Chi-square test of independence
options.C: Independent samples t-test
options.D: Paired samples t-test

explanation: Paired t-tests are used when the same subjects are measured twice under different conditions. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h4)

question: An independent samples t-test is used for which type of study design?

options.A: Measuring one group at three different times
options.B: Counting frequencies of disease outbreaks
options.C: Comparing two separate groups of patients
options.D: Observing a single patient over a whole year

explanation: Independent t-tests analyze two distinct, unrelated groups to see if their averages differ. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h4)

question: What does a larger t-statistic generally indicate about two groups?

options.A: A greater difference between their means
options.B: A failure to meet normal distribution
options.C: A higher rate of dropouts in the trial
options.D: A smaller overall sample size in the study

explanation: The t-statistic grows larger when the distance between group averages increases relative to data variability. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h5)

question: The denominator of the t-test formula primarily accounts for which factor?

options.A: The total number of hospital wards
options.B: The duration of the nursing shift
options.C: The exact cost of the medical intervention
options.D: Variability within the sample groups

explanation: The denominator measures sample variance or spread, which helps scale the difference between means. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h5)

question: What is the standard p-value threshold used to determine statistical significance in healthcare?
explanation: A p-value of less than 0.05 is the conventional cutoff for rejecting the null hypothesis. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h6)

question: A calculated p-value of 0.02 means what about the study results?

options.A: There is a 2% chance the results occurred by random error
options.B: The null hypothesis must be accepted as absolute truth
options.C: The sample size used in the study was far too small
options.D: The intervention was effective in 98% of all hospitals

explanation: A p-value represents the exact probability of obtaining the observed results purely by chance. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h6)

question: Why must nurses distinguish between statistical significance and clinical importance?

options.A: Patient samples never reflect real-world nursing conditions
options.B: Clinical importance only matters when p-values are ignored
options.C: A statistically significant difference might be too small to help patients
options.D: Statistical tests cannot be used in actual hospital wards

explanation: Massive sample sizes can make trivial medical differences look statistically significant without practical clinical value. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h7)

question: A research article reports a new wound healing cream reduced healing time with p < 0.01. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Assume the data proves the cream works for every disease
options.B: Ignore the finding because p-values are never reliable
options.C: Discard the study because it used an independent t-test
options.D: Consider adopting the practice based on strong evidence

explanation: A low p-value indicates reliable research findings that can support evidence-based nursing interventions. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T14#GNS217_U4_T14_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of hypothesis testing in nursing research?

options.A: To replace the need for collecting patient sample data
options.B: To evaluate if clinical interventions genuinely improve patient outcomes
options.C: To prove that two nursing variables are identical
options.D: To eliminate all possible errors in a clinical study

explanation: Hypothesis testing uses statistical analysis to determine whether observed changes in patient outcomes result from an intervention or random chance. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h1)

question: A researcher wants to know if a new wound care protocol speeds up healing. What starts this investigative process?

options.A: The rejection of all samples
options.B: A proven type II error
options.C: A specific clinical question
options.D: The final statistical p-value

explanation: Every formal hypothesis testing process begins by translating a practical clinical question into testable statements. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h1)

question: The null hypothesis always assumes which of the following conditions?

options.A: The sample size is too small to calculate
options.B: No difference or effect exists between groups
options.C: The alternative hypothesis is always correct
options.D: A major clinical improvement has occurred

explanation: The null hypothesis serves as a baseline statement proposing that any observed differences are due to random chance rather than an intervention. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h2)

question: A nurse researcher believes a new pain management protocol lowers blood pressure. How is this belief written?

options.A: As the null hypothesis
options.B: As the alternative hypothesis
options.C: As a type I error
options.D: As a significance level

explanation: The researcher's prediction that an intervention has an effect represents the alternative hypothesis. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h2)

question: What is a Type I error in nursing research?

options.A: Selecting a sample size that is too large
options.B: Calculating the p-value incorrectly
options.C: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
options.D: Rejecting a true null hypothesis

explanation: A Type I error happens when a study mistakenly claims an intervention works when it actually has no real effect. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h3)

question: A clinical study concludes that a new bandage prevents infection when it actually does not. What kind of error is this?

options.A: Type II error
options.B: Type I error
options.C: Null error
options.D: Sample error

explanation: Concluding that an ineffective treatment works results in a false positive, which defines a Type I error. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h3)

question: What does a standard significance level of 0.05 mean in a study?

options.A: The research hypothesis has a 95 percent chance of failure
options.B: The p-value is automatically set to zero
options.C: The sample size must contain at least 5 patients
options.D: A 5 percent risk of a Type I error is accepted

explanation: The alpha level establishes the acceptable threshold for mistakenly rejecting a true null hypothesis. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h4)

question: When is a null hypothesis rejected based on the calculated p-value?

options.A: When the p-value equals exactly one
options.B: When the p-value is greater than the sample size
options.C: When the p-value is less than or equal to alpha
options.D: When the significance level is omitted

explanation: A small p-value indicates that the data are unlikely under the null hypothesis, justifying its rejection. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h4)

question: Which statistical test is best suited for comparing the mean test scores of two separate patient groups?

options.A: ANOVA
options.B: Null test
options.C: T-test
options.D: Chi-square test

explanation: A t-test evaluates whether the means of two independent groups are statistically different from each other. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h5)

question: A nurse is analyzing categorical survey data about patient smoking status. Which test should be used?

options.A: Chi-square test
options.B: Alpha test
options.C: ANOVA
options.D: T-test

explanation: Chi-square tests are designed specifically to analyze categorical or frequency data. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h5)

question: Why must a nurse look beyond a statistically significant p-value when reading a research paper?

options.A: Clinical relevance is always higher than statistical tests
options.B: Statistical significance does not guarantee clinical usefulness
options.C: A low p-value means the study had too few patients
options.D: The null hypothesis cannot be proven in a hospital setting

explanation: An intervention can show a statistically significant difference that is too small to make any meaningful improvement in patient care. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h6)

question: A study reports a statistically significant reduction in recovery time of two minutes for a costly surgical procedure. What should the nurse manager consider?

options.A: If the researchers committed a Type I error by using a t-test
options.B: Why the null hypothesis was not accepted automatically
options.C: Whether the significance level should be changed to 0.10
options.D: Whether a two-minute improvement justifies the extra cost

explanation: Clinical decision-making requires weighing the practical impact and cost against the statistical findings. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of descriptive statistics in research?

options.A: To test complex clinical hypotheses
options.B: To predict future patient outcomes
options.C: To summarize and organize raw data
options.D: To prove a cause-and-effect relationship

explanation: Descriptive statistics focus entirely on organizing, summarizing, and presenting raw data in a clear, understandable format. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T2#GNS217_U4_T2_h1)

question: A ward manager calculates the average length of stay for malaria patients. This task represents which type of statistics?

options.A: Descriptive statistics
options.B: Qualitative statistics
options.C: Experimental statistics
options.D: Inferential statistics

explanation: Calculating an average for a specific group of patients already studied falls directly under descriptive statistics. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T2#GNS217_U4_T2_h1)
