options.D: To help the researcher stay focused on finding direct answers and proper statistics

explanation: Exactly! Specific objectives keep your study tightly focused on testing cause and effect without getting distracted. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h2)

question: What type of data is mostly used in explanatory research designs?

options.A: Numerical measurements and statistical testing
options.B: Only handwritten personal diaries from patients
options.C: Random historical fiction books
options.D: Unstructured gossip from hospital hallways

explanation: Well done! Explanatory designs use numbers and statistics to clearly show cause-and-effect links. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h3)

question: Why is controlling outside factors so important in explanatory research?

options.A: To guarantee that patients refuse to participate in the study
options.B: To ensure that the observed changes are truly caused by the studied variable
options.C: To hide negative outcomes from the hospital administration
options.D: To make the research process take as long as humanly possible

explanation: You got it! Controlling outside noise makes sure your results genuinely reflect the cause-and-effect you are testing. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h3)

question: Which research design is best for answering 'Why or how does this event happen?'

options.A: Explanatory design
options.B: Descriptive design
options.C: Historical design
options.D: Exploratory design

explanation: Brilliant! Explanatory research is built specifically to uncover the 'why' and 'how' behind health events. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h4)

question: A nurse wants to document the exact number of malaria cases in a clinic last month. Which study type fits best?

options.A: Experimental laboratory design
options.B: Descriptive design
options.C: Explanatory design
options.D: Exploratory design

explanation: Correct! When you are just describing what is happening naturally without testing causes, it's a descriptive study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h4)

question: What is the term for the variable that acts as the final measured outcome in a study?

options.A: Confounding variable
options.B: Dependent variable
options.C: Extraneous variable
options.D: Independent variable

explanation: You're doing great! The dependent variable is your final outcome that changes in response to what you tested. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h5)

question: How does having a clear hypothesis help a nurse researcher?

options.A: It guarantees that funding will be instantly approved by the government
options.B: It provides a clear prediction of expected relationships to guide testing
options.C: It stops patients from withdrawing their consent midway through
options.D: It eliminates the need for any statistical calculations at the end

explanation: Spot on! A hypothesis gives your study a roadmap so you know exactly what relationship you are testing. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h5)

question: Why must the tools used to collect data in explanatory research be valid and reliable?

options.A: To prevent the hospital from paying research fees
options.B: To ensure the measurements are accurate and trustworthy
options.C: To reduce the total number of participants required
options.D: To make sure the questionnaires are printed in full color

explanation: Awesome! Reliable tools mean your measurements can be trusted and will give consistent results every time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a good practice when collecting data for an explanatory study?

options.A: Changing the measurement questions halfway through the study to suit new patients
options.B: Using standardized scales for every single participating subject
options.C: Ensuring tools accurately capture the variables being tested
options.D: Maintaining consistency across all data gathering sessions

explanation: That's right! Changing your questions halfway through ruins your consistency and messes up your findings. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h6)

question: What type of statistics is mainly used in explanatory research to test hypotheses?

options.A: Decorative statistics
options.B: Inferential statistics
options.C: Fictional statistics
options.D: Historical statistics

explanation: You've got it! Inferential statistics help us test hypotheses and check if our findings are truly significant. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h7)

question: Why are basic averages and percentages not enough on their own for explanatory research?

options.A: They can only be calculated by certified medical doctors
options.B: They are completely illegal to use in modern nursing journals
options.C: They do not prove whether one variable directly caused a change in another
options.D: They require computers that are too expensive for standard hospitals

explanation: Brilliant! Averages only describe numbers, but explanatory research needs deeper tests to prove cause and effect. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h7)

question: What is a major strength of using explanatory research in healthcare?

options.A: They require zero effort to plan and execute
options.B: They allow researchers to skip informed consent
options.C: They completely eliminate all hospital financial costs
options.D: They provide clear evidence for clinical interventions

explanation: Spot on! The biggest win of explanatory research is generating solid evidence to upgrade patient care. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h8)

question: Why must nurse researchers pay close attention to ethics during explanatory studies?

options.A: Because ethics boards only approve studies written in foreign languages
options.B: Because testing new interventions or manipulating variables can potentially affect patient safety
options.C: Because hospital patients prefer answering long questionnaires over resting
options.D: Because research ethics only apply to doctors and never to nurses

explanation: You nailed it! Whenever we test new methods or change care routines, keeping our patients safe is always the top priority. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h8)

question: What is the primary starting point for a retrospective research design?

options.A: A prospective patient interview process
options.B: A newly planned clinical intervention
options.C: An outcome that has already occurred
options.D: An active laboratory experiment on animals

explanation: Retrospective studies look backward in time from an established outcome to find preceding causes or factors. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h1)

question: How does a retrospective study differ fundamentally from a prospective study?

options.A: It looks at past events instead of following subjects forward.
options.B: It only uses qualitative interviews instead of quantitative data.
options.C: It eliminates the need for any ethical clearance approval.
options.D: It requires direct patient participation and live clinical trials.

explanation: Retrospective designs evaluate historical data, whereas prospective designs follow subjects forward in real time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h1)

question: What direction does the inquiry move in a retrospective study?

options.A: Backward from effect to cause
options.B: Sideways across multiple communities
options.C: Directly through live experimental trials
options.D: Forward from exposure to disease

explanation: The researcher identifies the outcome first and looks backward in records to find the initial exposure or cause. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h2)

question: Why is a retrospective study considered an observational design?

options.A: The investigator actively controls the clinical environment.
options.B: The nurse must observe patients live on the hospital ward.
options.C: The researcher does not manipulate variables or assign treatments.
options.D: The study requires direct visual observation of drug administration.

explanation: Observational designs rely on recording existing events or conditions without the researcher intervening or altering treatment. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h2)

question: Which retrospective design compares patients with a specific condition against those without it?

options.A: Case-control study
options.B: Randomized trial
options.C: Qualitative interview
options.D: Prospective cohort

explanation: Case-control studies select individuals with a specific outcome and compare them to controls without that outcome. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h3)

question: A nurse researcher examines past records to compare patients with wound infections to those without infections regarding previous antibiotic use. What type of study is this?

options.A: Prospective survey
options.B: Case-control study
options.C: Experimental trial
options.D: Case report study

explanation: Comparing a group with an outcome to a group without an outcome to look at past exposures defines a case-control design. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h3)

question: What is a primary data source for conducting retrospective nursing research?

options.A: Real-time focus groups
options.B: Patient medical records
options.C: Live clinical observations
options.D: Active laboratory trials

explanation: Medical records provide the historical documentation necessary for reviewing past patient care and outcomes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h4)

question: Why do researchers use standardized abstraction forms during retrospective data collection?

options.A: To ensure consistent data gathering across all reviewed charts
options.B: To replace the need for institutional ethical approval letters
options.C: To allow patients to update their personal health history live
options.D: To actively manipulate clinical variables during the review

explanation: Standardized forms ensure every record is evaluated using the exact same criteria, reducing data collection errors. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h4)

question: Which benefit is a major advantage of retrospective research designs?

options.A: They require zero ethical review board approvals.
options.B: They are typically cost-effective and fast to complete.
options.C: They allow researchers to actively control clinical variables.
options.D: They completely eliminate all forms of measurement bias.

explanation: Because the data is already collected, retrospective studies save considerable time and financial resources. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h5)

question: Why are retrospective designs particularly useful when studying rare medical conditions?

options.A: Prospective follow-up takes only a few days for rare disorders.
options.B: Patients with rare conditions are easier to recruit for live interviews.
options.C: Rare diseases never appear in historical records or electronic databases.
options.D: Existing hospital archives already contain accumulated cases over many years.

explanation: Pooling historical records allows researchers to gather enough cases of rare conditions that would take too long to find prospectively. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h5)

question: What type of bias occurs when participants inaccurately remember past events?

options.A: Recall bias
options.B: Attrition bias
options.C: Selection bias
options.D: Allocation bias

explanation: Recall bias happens when study participants or staff have trouble accurately remembering details from the past. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h6)

question: Which of the following is a major challenge when using historical nursing records for research?

options.A: Patients refuse to participate in live clinical examinations.
options.B: The researcher actively alters the past treatment given.
options.C: Incomplete charting leaves missing gaps in the required data.
options.D: Prospective follow-up timelines become too long to manage.

explanation: Past documentation is often prone to omissions, making missing data a frequent hurdle in retrospective reviews. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h6)

question: What must be secured before accessing hospital records for a retrospective study?

options.A: Immediate funding from international donors
options.B: Ethical committee approval
options.C: Verbal consent from hospital directors
options.D: Live consent from every ward nurse

explanation: Formal ethical clearance is mandatory for any research utilizing patient health records, regardless of study design. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h7)

question: Why is data anonymization crucial when conducting retrospective chart reviews?

options.A: To allow researchers to contact patients directly for live interviews
options.B: To protect patient confidentiality and prevent exposure of personal health information
options.C: To speed up the statistical analysis process on hospital computers
options.D: To eliminate the possibility of missing data in the medical chart

explanation: Removing identifying details ensures patients' privacy is maintained when their historical records are analyzed. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h7)

question: What should be established first before reviewing any patient records in a study?

options.A: Final publication manuscript draft
options.B: Research question and hypothesis
options.C: Statistical software installation
options.D: Patient interview appointment times

explanation: A clear research question must guide the scope and direction of any data collection process. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h8)

question: Why are explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria necessary for selecting patient files?

options.A: To allow the researcher to alter past patient treatments
options.B: To guarantee that zero data points will ever be missing
options.C: To eliminate the need for institutional ethical clearance
options.D: To ensure only relevant and appropriate records are evaluated

explanation: Clear criteria ensure consistency and validity by defining precisely which records belong in the study population. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h8)

question: What is the primary direction of time in a prospective research design?

options.A: Moving backward from the present into the past
options.B: Comparing two different time periods in history
options.C: Moving forward from the present into the future
options.D: Examining past medical records for current outcomes

explanation: Prospective studies are designed to follow participants forward in time to observe future outcomes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h1)

question: How does a prospective study differ fundamentally from a retrospective study?

options.A: Prospective studies look forward at future events, while retrospective studies look backward at past records
options.B: Prospective studies involve no data collection, while retrospective studies involve heavy data collection
options.C: Prospective studies are always qualitative, while retrospective studies are always quantitative
options.D: Prospective studies use animal subjects, while retrospective studies only use human patients

explanation: The core difference lies in the temporal orientation, with prospective starting in the present and moving forward, and retrospective starting in the present and looking backward. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h1)

question: What is the most common type of prospective observational study used in healthcare research?

options.A: Cross-sectional survey
options.B: Cohort study
options.C: Historical review
options.D: Case report

explanation: Cohort studies follow groups of participants over time to observe the development of specific health outcomes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h2)

question: Why is a randomized controlled trial considered a prospective design?

options.A: It applies an intervention in the present and follows participants forward to measure the results
options.B: It looks only at events that happened before the study started
options.C: It avoids following patients over time by using computer simulations
options.D: It gathers all of its data from hospital files written ten years ago

explanation: Clinical trials require a forward-looking timeline to measure how patients respond to a newly introduced treatment or nursing intervention. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h2)

question: Why is recall bias significantly reduced in prospective studies?

options.A: Researchers only interview family members instead of the actual patients
options.B: Medical records are automatically encrypted to prevent human memory errors
options.C: Data is collected in real-time rather than asking people to remember past events
options.D: Participants are hypnotized to forget their previous medical history

explanation: Because information is gathered as events happen, researchers do not depend on flawed human memory of past exposures. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h3)

question: A nurse researcher wants to prove that a new wound care protocol prevents infections better than the old method without relying on messy old records. Which study design should be chosen?

options.A: Prospective design
options.B: Cross-sectional snapshot
options.C: Case-control past analysis
options.D: Retrospective chart review

explanation: A prospective design allows the researcher to implement the protocol today and record infection rates moving forward with high accuracy. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h3)

question: What is a major reason why prospective studies are poorly suited for investigating rare diseases?

options.A: Patients with rare diseases refuse to answer questionnaires
options.B: Ethics committees completely forbid studying rare conditions prospectively
options.C: Researchers would need to follow an enormous number of people for many years to see enough cases
options.D: Computers cannot store data collected over a long period

explanation: Rare diseases occur so infrequently that a prospective study would require an unfeasibly large sample size and long timeframe to capture enough events. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h4)

question: What does 'loss to follow-up' mean in the context of a longitudinal prospective study?

options.A: Nurses forget to check the patient's vital signs during a routine shift
options.B: Participants drop out, move away, or stop responding before the research is completed
options.C: Researchers accidentally delete all computer files from the first day of the study
options.D: The hospital misplaces the budget allocated for patient transportation

explanation: Attrition threatens study validity when participants who leave differ systematically from those who stay until the final evaluation. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h4)

question: Which strategy is most effective for reducing participant drop-out in a long-term prospective nursing study?

options.A: Changing the research topic every month without telling the participants
options.B: Restricting participant access to their own health records
options.C: Punishing patients who miss a single clinical check-up appointment
options.D: Maintaining regular communication and providing appointment reminders

explanation: Consistent contact and thoughtful reminders help keep participants committed and reachable throughout a long study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h5)

question: Why is gathering comprehensive baseline data essential at the very start of a prospective study?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any further follow-up appointments
options.B: It allows researchers to alter the inclusion criteria midway through the study
options.C: It establishes a clear, accurate starting point to compare against future changes
options.D: It guarantees that no participants will ever drop out of the project

explanation: Accurate baseline measurements are necessary to accurately measure how much change occurs over time in the subsequent follow-up phases. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h5)

question: What key right must be explicitly explained to participants before they enter a prospective study?

options.A: The obligation to pay for any specialized diagnostic tests
options.B: The requirement to remain in the project until final publication
options.C: The promise that no adverse events will ever occur
options.D: The right to withdraw from the study at any time without penalty

explanation: Voluntary participation means individuals can exit a research study whenever they choose without losing access to standard medical care. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h6)

question: What ethical action must nurse researchers take if an intervention being tested in a prospective trial proves to be significantly harmful?

options.A: Ask participants to sign a waiver accepting the new dangers
options.B: Hide the adverse results until the final academic paper is published
options.C: Continue the trial until the originally scheduled end date anyway
options.D: Stop the trial immediately to protect participants from further harm

explanation: Researcher safety oversight demands that patient welfare always supersedes study completion if unexpected dangers emerge. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h6)

question: How do prospective study findings directly benefit frontline nurses working in clinical wards?

options.A: By providing historical background on ancient medical discoveries
options.B: By eliminating the need for patient assessments during night shifts
options.C: By replacing all bedside charting with automated computer algorithms
options.D: By helping identify high-risk patients early so preventative nursing care can be applied

explanation: Prospective research uncovers risk factors that frontline nurses use to spot vulnerable patients and prevent adverse hospital events. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h7)

question: A head nurse wants to know if a newly introduced fall-prevention bundle actually decreases patient falls over the next year on the surgical ward. Which action represents applying prospective thinking?

options.A: Implementing the bundle today and tracking fall rates prospectively over the coming year
options.B: Interviewing staff nurses about falls that occurred before they were born
options.C: Asking elderly patients to guess why they might fall in the future
options.D: Looking up incident reports from five years ago to see how many people slipped

explanation: Applying a measure today and observing future outcomes embodies the core methodology of prospective clinical research. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h7)

question: In nursing research, what do we mean by the word 'population'?

options.A: Every person living in the city where the study takes place
options.B: The specific patients who dropped out of a clinical trial
options.C: The entire group of people the researcher wants to study
options.D: Only the nurses working in a specific hospital ward

explanation: You've got this! In research, the 'population' is just the big group of people you are curious about and want to learn more from. Think of it as the big picture before you zoom in. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h1)

question: Why is it super important for a nurse researcher to clearly define their study population?

options.A: It ensures that every person in the country gets surveyed
options.B: It eliminates all possible errors in data collection
options.C: It reduces the financial cost of printing research papers
options.D: It helps them know exactly who the final study results will apply to

explanation: Spot on! When you know your exact population, you can proudly say who your findings will help in everyday hospital or community practice. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h1)

question: What is the main difference between a target population and an accessible population?

options.A: The target population is smaller than the accessible population
options.B: The accessible population includes dead patients, but the target population does not
options.C: There is no difference between these two terms in nursing studies
options.D: The target population is the ideal group, while the accessible group can actually be reached

explanation: Great thinking! The target group is your dream group (everyone with the condition), while the accessible group is the realistic bunch right there in your hospital that you can actually talk to and study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h2)

question: A nurse wants to study pregnant women nationwide, but she only collects data from patients at her own clinic. What is her clinic patient group called?

options.A: The control population
options.B: The accessible population
options.C: The sampling frame
options.D: The target population

explanation: Exactly! They are your accessible population because they are right there in your clinic, ready and easy for you to reach for your study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h2)

question: What is the main job of 'inclusion criteria' in a nursing research study?

options.A: To explain how data will be analyzed using statistical software
options.B: To define the specific traits a participant must have to join the study
options.C: To list the reasons why a patient should be given extra medication
options.D: To describe the equipment used to measure patient vital signs

explanation: You nailed it! Inclusion criteria are simply the 'welcome checklist' of traits a person must have to be part of your research. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h3)

question: Why do researchers use exclusion criteria when picking study participants?

options.A: To keep out factors that could mess up the study results or harm the patient
options.B: To remove the need for getting informed consent from patients
options.C: To increase the total number of people in the research study
options.D: To make sure every nurse in the hospital gets a chance to participate

explanation: Well done! Exclusion criteria act like a safety guard, keeping out things that might confuse your results or put a vulnerable patient at risk. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h3)

question: In research language, what is a 'sampling frame'?

options.A: A framework for writing up the final research report
options.B: The physical room where patient interviews take place
options.C: A complete list of everyone in the accessible population
options.D: The statistical formula used to calculate sample size

explanation: Think of a sampling frame as your phone book or registry list. It's the actual directory of names you draw your participants from! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h4)

question: Which of these best describes probability sampling?

options.A: Participants are chosen simply because they are easy to find and talk to
options.B: The researcher hand-picks participants who agree with their hypothesis
options.C: Every member of the population has a known chance of being selected
options.D: Only patients with severe symptoms are allowed to join the study

explanation: Awesome! Probability sampling uses fairness and randomization, meaning nobody is unfairly favored and everyone has an equal shot at being picked. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h4)

question: What can happen if a nursing research study uses a sample size that is far too small?

options.A: The statistical software will refuse to run any calculations
options.B: Every patient in the hospital will be forced to participate
options.C: The researcher might miss a real and important clinical effect
options.D: The study will automatically cost too much money to complete

explanation: Spot on! If your group of patients is too tiny, your study won't have enough power to spot a real pattern or treatment benefit. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h5)

question: How do researchers know when they have enough participants in a qualitative nursing study?

options.A: By using a complex mathematical formula before the study begins
options.B: By selecting exactly fifty participants for every single project
options.C: By continuing interviews until data saturation is reached
options.D: By stopping when the research budget runs out of funds

explanation: You got it! In qualitative studies, you keep talking to people until you stop hearing anything new—that's called reaching 'data saturation'. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h5)

question: What does 'generalizability' mean in a nursing research study?

options.A: The general health status of patients before they enter a trial
options.B: Whether the hospital director approves the nursing research project
options.C: The speed at which a research paper gets published in a journal
options.D: How well study results from a sample apply to the broader population

explanation: Brilliant! Generalizability is all about whether the good things you discovered from studying a small group of patients will also hold true for patients everywhere else. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to avoid bias when picking patients for a study?

options.A: Hand-picking only the friendliest patients to answer questionnaires
options.B: Clearly defining inclusion and exclusion rules before starting
options.C: Ensuring that diverse patient sub-groups are properly represented
options.D: Using a random number generator to pick names from a patient registry

explanation: You're doing great! Hand-picking only your favorite or friendliest patients introduces bias because it doesn't give everyone a fair and equal chance to participate. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h6)

question: Why do nurse researchers usually study a smaller sample instead of tracking every single patient in the country?

options.A: It ensures that zero ethical approvals are required from the hospital
options.B: It guarantees that every single patient receives direct medical treatment
options.C: It completely eliminates all forms of human error in data collection
options.D: It saves time, money, and resources while still providing useful data

explanation: Spot on! Trying to study an entire population is almost always impossible. Taking a smaller, well-chosen sample makes your research practical and achievable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h1)

question: In research terms, how does a 'sample' connect to a 'population'?

options.A: The sample is a smaller, manageable subset chosen to represent the broader population
options.B: The population and the sample must always contain the exact same number of people
options.C: The sample includes every single individual who has ever had the medical condition
options.D: The population is just a pilot group tested before the main sample is selected

explanation: You got it! We study the smaller group (the sample) so we can figure out what is happening in the big group (the population) without getting overwhelmed. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h1)

question: What do we mean by the 'target population' in a research project?

options.A: The patients who successfully complete every single day of the treatment trial
options.B: The ideal, entire group of people the researcher wants to apply findings to
options.C: The small group of nurses who help collect data at the clinic desk
options.D: The government officials who give permission to run the hospital study

explanation: Exactly! The target population is your ultimate group of interest—even if you can't physically reach every single one of them. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h2)

question: How is an 'accessible population' different from a 'target population'?

options.A: much larger and broader than the original target group
options.B: exempt from standard hospital ethical clearance procedures
options.C: composed entirely of medical doctors rather than everyday patients
options.D: physically available and realistic for the researcher to recruit

explanation: Spot on! The target group is your dream group, but the accessible group is the practical batch of patients you can actually walk up to and recruit in your hospital. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h2)

question: What is the main job of 'inclusion criteria' when setting up a nursing study?

options.A: To increase the financial cost of running the clinical trial for the hospital
options.B: To punish patients who refuse to take their prescribed routine medications
options.C: To list every single complication that happened during the hospital admission
options.D: To define the specific characteristics a participant must possess to join the study

explanation: Well done! Inclusion criteria act like a checklist of traits a person must have to qualify for your research. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h3)

question: Which of these is a clear example of using 'exclusion criteria'?

options.A: Leaving out patients who already have a severe kidney disease from a drug trial
options.B: Increasing the sample size after finding out the first group was too small
options.C: Admitting every patient who walks through the outpatient clinic door
options.D: Asking participants to write down their home addresses on a survey form

explanation: Exactly! Exclusion criteria help filter out people who might get harmed by the study or mess up the results. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h3)

question: What makes 'probability sampling' special compared to other methods?

options.A: The researcher hand-picks participants who have the most interesting medical history
options.B: Every individual in the population has a known, random chance of being selected
options.C: Participants are recruited strictly on a first-come, first-served hospital entry basis
options.D: Only the most cooperative patients on the hospital ward are chosen to participate

explanation: You nailed it! Probability sampling relies on pure chance, meaning everyone in the group has a fair and calculable shot at being picked. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h4)

question: A nurse researcher splits a hospital's staff into day-shift and night-shift groups, then randomly picks nurses from both. What sampling method is this?

options.A: Snowball sampling
options.B: Quota sampling
options.C: Stratified random sampling
options.D: Convenience sampling

explanation: Brilliant! Dividing people into meaningful groups (strata) like shifts and then picking randomly from each is stratified sampling. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h4)

question: Which sampling technique simply grabs participants because they are easy to reach and right in front of you?

options.A: Systematic sampling
options.B: Stratified sampling
options.C: Cluster sampling
options.D: Convenience sampling

explanation: Spot on! Convenience sampling uses whoever is readily available—like patients sitting right now in your clinic waiting room. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h5)

question: A researcher studying a rare illness asks current patients to bring in friends or family members with the same condition. What is this called?

options.A: Quota sampling
options.B: Simple random sampling
options.C: Snowball sampling
options.D: Systematic sampling

explanation: You got it! Just like a snowball rolling downhill gets bigger, participants help you recruit more participants from their network. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h5)

question: In health research, what is the standard benchmark usually accepted for statistical power?
explanation: Good memory! A power of 0.80 means your study has an 80% chance of catching a real treatment effect if it's actually there. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h6)

question: What is the biggest danger of running a nursing study with a sample size that is way too small?

options.A: Making the data analysis so complex that computers take days to run it
options.B: Failing to get approval from the hospital ethics and research board
options.C: Missing a real treatment effect or clinical difference due to lack of power
options.D: Incurring massive financial debt from buying unnecessary hospital supplies

explanation: Exactly! Small samples are too weak to show the truth, often tricking researchers into thinking a great intervention didn't work when it actually did. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h6)

question: What is the main difference between sampling error and sampling bias?

options.A: Sampling error only happens in qualitative studies, while bias happens in quantitative studies
options.B: Sampling error is caused by dishonest participants, while bias is caused by computer glitches
options.C: Sampling bias can be completely avoided with large samples, while error cannot be fixed
options.D: Sampling error is natural random variation, while sampling bias is a systematic flaw in selection

explanation: Spot on! Error is just normal luck of the draw, but bias means your method had a unfair lean that messed up the results. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to manage or reduce sampling issues?

options.A: Using a larger sample size to decrease natural random sampling error
options.B: Employing random selection methods to give every patient an equal chance
options.C: Purposely selecting only wealthy patients to make hospital data look prestigious
options.D: Setting strict inclusion and exclusion criteria to keep participant groups clear

explanation: You got it! Hand-picking a specific group to make things look good introduces terrible bias instead of fixing research problems. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h7)

question: Why do nurse researchers use sampling in their studies?

options.A: To study a smaller group to represent a larger population
options.B: To reduce the cost of printing questionnaires only
options.C: To make every patient in a hospital participate
options.D: To eliminate all possible errors in a study

explanation: Spot on! Studying everyone is nearly impossible, so sampling helps us pick a manageable group that mirrors the whole population. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h1)

question: Why is studying an entire population usually impractical for a nursing study?

options.A: Research ethics committees do not allow large studies
options.B: Patients refuse to answer questions if everyone is included
options.C: Statistical software cannot process large amounts of data
options.D: It is too expensive, time-consuming, and logistically difficult

explanation: Exactly! Imagine trying to interview every single nurse or patient in the whole country—you'd spend all your time and money moving around. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h1)

question: What exactly is a 'sampling frame' in research?

options.A: The final group of patients selected for a clinical trial
options.B: The statistical formula used to calculate sample size
options.C: A physical list of all eligible members in a target population
options.D: A barrier preventing patients from joining a study

explanation: You got it! Think of the sampling frame as your actual register, directory, or database from which you pull your participants. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h2)

question: A researcher wants to study nurses in Abuja and gets the official staff register from the ministry. What is this register called?

options.A: The final sample
options.B: The inclusion criteria
options.C: The sampling frame
options.D: The target population

explanation: Spot on! That staff register serves as the concrete list you draw your participants from, making it your sampling frame. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h2)

question: Which sampling method involves picking every 5th or 10th person from an organized list?

options.A: Systematic sampling
options.B: Simple random sampling
options.C: Stratified sampling
options.D: Convenience sampling

explanation: Brilliant! Systematic sampling means you use a fixed math interval (like every 10th nurse on the roster) after a random start. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h3)

question: A researcher groups hospital nurses into junior, senior, and management ranks, then picks randomly from each group. What method is this?

options.A: Systematic sampling
options.B: Convenience sampling
options.C: Stratified random sampling
options.D: Cluster sampling

explanation: Correct! When you divide people into subgroups (strata) first, you ensure every important level is fairly represented in your study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h3)

question: What is the main idea behind convenience sampling?

options.A: Using a computer program to select names randomly
options.B: Asking participants to refer other qualified friends
options.C: Dividing the population into equal demographic groups
options.D: Choosing participants who are easiest to reach and recruit

explanation: You nailed it! Convenience sampling is all about grabbing whoever is readily available—like the students sitting right next to you in class. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h4)

question: Studying a rare medical condition, a researcher asks early patients to connect her with other patients they know. What technique is this?

options.A: Snowball sampling
options.B: Quota sampling
options.C: Stratified sampling
options.D: Systematic sampling

explanation: Spot on! Just like a snowball rolls and gets bigger, your participant list grows as each person refers you to the next. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h4)

question: Why do researchers often recruit more people than their minimum calculated sample size?

options.A: To increase the chance of getting statistically insignificant results
options.B: To account for participants who drop out or withdraw during the study
options.C: To satisfy hospital administrators who love large group numbers
options.D: To make the data entry process longer for student assistants

explanation: Exactly! People travel, fall ill, or change their minds. Adding a buffer upfront saves your project if participants drop out. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h5)

question: How does population diversity affect the sample size you need for a study?

options.A: Diversity has no impact on the required number of participants
options.B: A more diverse population requires a smaller sample size
options.C: Diverse populations can only be studied using convenience sampling
options.D: A more diverse population requires a larger sample size

explanation: You got it! If the group has many different backgrounds and experiences, you need a bigger sample to capture all those variations accurately. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h5)

question: What actually happens when there is 'sampling bias' in research?

options.A: An error caused by using a broken weighing scale in the clinic
options.B: The refusal of patients to answer personal questions in a survey
options.C: A systematic flaw that favors certain individuals over others in selection
options.D: The natural mathematical difference between a sample and a population

explanation: Spot on! Sampling bias means your selection method accidentally gives some people a better chance of being picked than others, skewing your results. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h6)

question: Which of these does NOT help reduce sampling error in a research project?

options.A: Applying proper random sampling techniques during selection
options.B: Reducing the overall sample size to make data collection faster
options.C: Using a well-calculated and sufficiently large sample size
options.D: Ensuring the sampling frame covers the entire target population

explanation: Correct! Shrinking your sample size actually makes sampling errors worse, not better. Bigger, well-chosen samples are more reliable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h6)

question: What does 'voluntary participation' mean when recruiting study participants?

options.A: Participants must be paid a large cash reward for joining the study
options.B: Patients must complete all questionnaires before leaving the hospital ward
options.C: Hospital management decides which patients are best suited for the study
options.D: Patients can choose to join or refuse without facing any negative consequences

explanation: Brilliant! Participation must always be completely free choice—no penalties, no pressure. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h7)

question: Why is it wrong for a nurse to tell patients their hospital care depends on joining a research study?

options.A: It increases the risk of random sampling error
options.B: It breaks the rules of simple random sampling
options.C: It makes the final sample size too large
options.D: It removes the element of voluntary consent through coercion

explanation: Spot on! Using your position of power to force or trick patients into research is unethical. Their healthcare must never be tied to a study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h7)

question: Which historic code was created after World War II to stop harmful human experiments and protect patient rights?

options.A: The Belmont Report
options.B: The Florence Nightingale Pledge
options.C: The Helsinki Declaration
options.D: The Nuremberg Code

explanation: Spot on! The Nuremberg Code was set up after WWII to make sure human experiments are truly voluntary and safe. You've got this! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h1)

question: Why do we have formal research guidelines like the Belmont Report in healthcare?

options.A: To help hospitals make more money
options.B: To prevent exploitation and protect human participants from harm
options.C: To guarantee positive study results
options.D: To speed up drug approvals

explanation: Exactly! Past abuses taught us that research participants need strong, guaranteed protection for their safety and rights. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h1)

question: Which ethical principle simply means a nurse or researcher must 'do no harm' to study participants?

options.A: Non-maleficence
options.B: Autonomy
options.C: Justice
options.D: Veracity

explanation: Well done! Non-maleficence is all about keeping patients safe and preventing any physical or emotional harm. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h2)

question: A researcher targets prisoners for a risky drug trial just because they are locked up and easy to reach. Which ethical rule is being broken?

options.A: Veracity
options.B: Justice
options.C: Autonomy
options.D: Beneficence

explanation: Spot on! Justice means fair selection, so vulnerable groups aren't unfairly dumped with all the riskiest studies. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h2)

question: What is informed consent truly about in clinical research?

options.A: An ongoing conversation between the researcher and the participant
options.B: A form filed away where patients never see it
options.C: A guarantee that the study will cure the patient
options.D: A one-time legal paper signed at the hospital door

explanation: You got it! Informed consent isn't just a paper signature; it is a continuous, friendly dialogue from start to finish. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h3)

question: What can a patient do at any time during a research study if they feel uncomfortable?

options.A: Demand extra financial payment
options.B: Change the research hypothesis
options.C: Prescribe medication to others
options.D: Withdraw from the study

explanation: Correct! Participation is completely voluntary. Patients can walk away whenever they want, no questions asked. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h3)

question: What is the main difference between privacy and confidentiality in research?

options.A: Privacy relates to blood samples, while confidentiality is for interviews
options.B: Privacy is a person's right to control their space, while confidentiality is our duty to protect their data
options.C: Privacy is optional, but confidentiality is required by law
options.D: Privacy applies only to doctors, while confidentiality applies to nurses

explanation: Spot on! Privacy belongs to the patient's personal boundaries, while confidentiality is our professional promise to keep their secrets safe. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h4)

question: As a nurse, which action best protects a research participant's confidentiality?

options.A: Sharing phone numbers with marketing companies
options.B: Leaving signed consent forms on the front desk
options.C: Discussing patient stories loudly in the hospital cafeteria
options.D: Removing names from data sheets and using code numbers instead

explanation: Brilliant! De-identifying data ensures no one can trace health records back to a real person. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h4)

question: Which of these groups is considered a vulnerable population needing extra research protection?

options.A: Licensed physicians
options.B: Children
options.C: Hospital administrators
options.D: Healthy adult researchers

explanation: Correct! Children cannot give adult consent and have limited autonomy, so we must protect them extra carefully. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h5)

question: Why do researchers weigh risks and benefits before starting a study?

options.A: To ensure the study benefits are much greater than any possible harm
options.B: To prove that clinical trials have zero risks
options.C: To calculate how much profit the hospital will make
options.D: To decide which participants get paid the most

explanation: You nailed it! Good research makes sure the valuable knowledge gained is worth any risks taken by the participants. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h5)

question: What is the primary job of an Institutional Review Board (IRB)?

options.A: Securing big money grants for labs
options.B: Writing nursing textbooks
options.C: Marketing new drugs to hospitals
options.D: Protecting the rights and safety of human research participants

explanation: Spot on! The IRB acts as a safety shield to ensure human subjects are treated ethically and safely. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h6)

question: You want to interview patients tomorrow for a project but haven't gotten IRB ethics approval yet. What should you do?

options.A: Ask the head nurse to bypass the ethics committee
options.B: Collect data fast before anyone notices
options.C: Stop and wait until official ethical clearance is granted
options.D: Go ahead with interviews if patients give verbal consent

explanation: Exactly right! Patient safety comes first—never start human research without proper ethical clearance. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h6)

question: Which of these actions is a serious example of research misconduct?

options.A: Giving participants the right to withdraw
options.B: Getting ethical clearance before collecting data
options.C: Keeping participant files in a secure, password folder
options.D: Making up survey results to match what you want to prove

explanation: Spot on! Inventing data is called fabrication, and it destroys scientific honesty. We always report true findings! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h7)

question: What is the difference between data fabrication and data falsification?

options.A: Fabrication applies to nursing, falsification applies to physics
options.B: Fabrication is inventing fake data, while falsification is altering real data
options.C: Fabrication is legal with IRB approval, falsification is never allowed
options.D: Fabrication is stealing text, falsification is stealing money

explanation: You got it! Fabrication means making numbers up from thin air, while falsification means tampering with real results. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T19#GNS224_U1_T19_h7)

question: What is the main reason we do nursing research?

options.A: To replace clinical judgement with computer software
options.B: To lower hospital operational costs for management
options.C: To gather evidence and improve patient care
options.D: To reduce the number of working hours in a ward

explanation: You got this! Nursing research is all about finding out what works best so we can give our patients the highest quality of care possible. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h1)

question: In a research project, what is the difference between methodology and methods?

options.A: There is no difference between the two terms in scientific writing
options.B: Methods are used only in qualitative studies while methodology is for laboratories
options.C: Methodology is the overall strategy while methods are the specific tools used
options.D: Methodology refers to patient consent and methods refer to data destruction

explanation: Think of methodology as your big-picture game plan, while your methods are the actual tools (like questionnaires) you use to get the job done! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h1)

question: When planning a study, what exactly is a research design?

options.A: The overall structural blueprint for conducting a study
options.B: A detailed biography of the principal investigator
options.C: The final bibliography list at the end of a thesis
options.D: The statistical software used to type the report

explanation: Spot on! The research design is your master plan that guides you step-by-step from start to finish. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h2)

question: Why do people often compare a research design to an architect's drawing?

options.A: It dictates the physical height and color of the hospital
options.B: It gives direction and structural stability to the investigation
options.C: It is only created by engineers rather than healthcare workers
options.D: It is drawn on large blueprint paper using physical ink

explanation: Just like a builder needs a solid blueprint to put up a safe house, a researcher needs a design to keep the study structured and valid. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h2)

question: Which of these is an example of a research design rather than a tool?

options.A: A laboratory test tube used to check blood sugar
options.B: The overall structural framework of the study
options.C: A structured questionnaire handed to patients
options.D: An audio recording device used during an interview

explanation: Great job! The overall framework is your design, while items like questionnaires and test tubes are the physical tools you use inside that design. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h3)

question: A nurse studies post-operative pain and uses a numeric pain rating scale to collect data. What is that pain scale?

options.A: The overarching strategy
options.B: The conceptual framework
options.C: A research method
options.D: The research design

explanation: You're getting it! The pain scale is a specific tool used to gather information, making it a research method. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is the main goal of using a solid, well-thought-out research design?

options.A: To minimize bias and maximize validity
options.B: To make the final research report longer and heavier
options.C: To increase the financial profit of the hospital
options.D: To eliminate the need for patient informed consent

explanation: Exactly! A good design keeps errors and bias out so we can truly trust the results we find. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why should a research design make it easy for others to repeat the study?

options.A: So other researchers can repeat the study and check the results
options.B: So the original author can publish the exact same paper twice
options.C: To reduce the cost of printing physical textbooks
options.D: To prevent patients from participating in future studies

explanation: That's right! When other nurses can repeat your study and get similar results, it proves the findings are trustworthy and strong. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h4)

question: Which quality of a study means that if you repeat it, you will get consistent results?

options.A: Reliability
options.B: Neutrality
options.C: Generalizability
options.D: Randomization

explanation: Spot on! Reliability means your tools and methods are dependable and give consistent answers every time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h5)

question: In research, what does 'generalizability' mean?

options.A: Using general medical terms instead of nursing jargon
options.B: Applying sample findings to a larger population
options.C: Keeping the research questions broad and vague
options.D: Ensuring all participants share the exact same age

explanation: You got it! Generalizability is about taking what we learned from a small group of patients and safely applying it to the wider patient community. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h5)

question: Which type of research focuses mostly on numbers, math, and statistics?

options.A: Quantitative
options.B: Ethnographic
options.C: Qualitative
options.D: Phenomenological

explanation: Fantastic! Think 'Q for Quantity'—quantitative research deals with numbers and statistical analysis. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the main focus of a phenomenological research design?

options.A: Counting the exact number of hospital readmissions
options.B: Exploring the lived experiences of individuals
options.C: Comparing surgical equipment costs across states
options.D: Testing chemical reactions in a laboratory setting

explanation: Well done! Phenomenology is all about diving deep into human stories and personal experiences to understand how people truly feel. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the most important thing to look at when choosing a research design?

options.A: The nature of the research question
options.B: The color of the hospital ward walls
options.C: The personal hobby of the lead nurse
options.D: The brand of computer in the office

explanation: Spot on! Your research question is the boss—it tells you whether you need an experiment, a survey, or an interview study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h7)

question: Why might ethical rules stop a nurse researcher from using an experimental design for certain topics?

options.A: Experimental designs always cost more money than hospitals have
options.B: Ethical committees only approve studies written in a foreign language
options.C: Patients refuse to answer questions if a design is experimental
options.D: Researchers cannot intentionally expose human patients to harm

explanation: Patient safety always comes first! If an experiment could put someone at risk, ethics boards require us to use safer, observational designs instead. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T2#GNS224_U1_T2_h7)

question: What is the main goal of collecting data in nursing research?

options.A: To replace the need for physical patient assessments
options.B: To punish staff who do not follow hospital rules
options.C: To gather information for answering research questions
options.D: To increase the cost of running healthcare facilities

explanation: Spot on! We collect data systematically so we can find clear answers to our research questions and ultimately improve patient care. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why is getting accurate data so important for evidence-based nursing practice?

options.A: It proves that old nursing theories are always completely wrong
options.B: It ensures clinical decisions are based on reliable facts
options.C: It guarantees that every patient will have a short hospital stay
options.D: It eliminates the need for nurses to document daily care

explanation: You got it! Accurate data gives us solid, trustworthy evidence to use when deciding the best care plans for our patients at the bedside. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h1)

question: When a researcher collects 'primary data', what are they doing?

options.A: Records taken from old hospital admission logs from ten years ago
options.B: Data published in international textbooks without any author names
options.C: Information collected directly by the researcher for the current study
options.D: Information guessed by the nurse without asking the patient

explanation: That's correct! Primary data is freshly gathered firsthand by the investigator specifically for their current study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h2)

question: A student nurse uses old patient charts from the archive to study infection rates from last year. What kind of data is this?

options.A: Primary data
options.B: Experimental data
options.C: Secondary data
options.D: Hypothetical data

explanation: Well done! Because the student is using pre-existing records gathered by someone else in the past, it's called secondary data. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h2)

question: Quantitative data collection focuses mainly on what type of information?

options.A: Emotions and deep feelings
options.B: Detailed personal life stories
options.C: Open-ended spoken interviews
options.D: Numbers and measurable variables

explanation: Spot on! Think of 'quantitative' as 'quantity'—it's all about numbers, counts, and measurements. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h3)

question: Why do we need to regularly check and calibrate equipment like blood pressure cuffs during a study?

options.A: To make the equipment change color during the procedure
options.B: To ensure patients do not feel any pain during the test
options.C: To reduce the total cost of buying new hospital items
options.D: To prevent faulty readings and keep measurements accurate

explanation: You nailed it! Regular calibration ensures our tools give us true and dependable numbers every single time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h3)

question: What is the primary focus of qualitative research methods?

options.A: Calculating patient weights on a digital scale
options.B: Exploring human experiences and meanings in depth
options.C: Measuring precise chemical levels in the blood
options.D: Counting the exact number of pills in a bottle

explanation: That's right! Qualitative research helps us understand people's feelings, stories, and subjective experiences. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h4)

question: Which data collection method involves a researcher joining a group setting to watch daily routines naturally?

options.A: Participant observation
options.B: Closed-ended numeric survey
options.C: Biochemical laboratory assay
options.D: Automated blood pressure reading

explanation: Correct! By joining in or quietly watching the natural environment, the researcher gets a real-world view of daily behaviors. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h4)

question: In research, what does the term 'reliability' mean?

options.A: Whether the tool measures what it is supposed to measure
options.B: The speed at which the patient answers interview questions
options.C: Consistency of results when using a tool repeatedly
options.D: How expensive the laboratory equipment is to purchase

explanation: Spot on! If a tool is reliable, it gives you stable, dependable results every time you use it under the same conditions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h5)

question: Why must all research assistants follow the exact same steps when collecting data?

options.A: To make the research study finish in a single afternoon
options.B: To eliminate the need for any written documentation
options.C: To ensure the patients finish their hospital meals faster
options.D: To prevent personal bias and reduce random measurement errors

explanation: You got it! Following a standard procedure ensures that everyone collects data the same way, keeping our results accurate and unbiased. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h5)

question: What must a researcher always get from a patient before collecting any study data?

options.A: Permission from local media
options.B: A monetary donation
options.C: Informed consent
options.D: Medical insurance cards

explanation: Correct! Patients must always voluntarily agree to take part after fully understanding what the study is about. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h6)

question: Which of these is the best way to protect patient privacy during data collection?

options.A: Replacing patient names with code numbers on data sheets
options.B: Leaving interview notebooks open on the nurses' station desk
options.C: Posting study results on public bulletin boards in the ward
options.D: Sharing patient diagnoses with visiting family members

explanation: Well done! Using code numbers instead of real names hides patient identities and keeps their personal information safe. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of doing a pilot test before starting the main study?

options.A: To identify confusing questions or faulty equipment early
options.B: To discharge all stable patients from the hospital ward
options.C: To increase the financial budget of the research project
options.D: To publish the final research paper in a medical journal

explanation: Spot on! A pilot test is like a practice run that helps us catch and fix any issues before the big study begins. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a good practice when collecting data?

options.A: Training all data collectors thoroughly before starting
options.B: Securing formal institutional approvals from management
options.C: Pilot testing questionnaires on a small sample group
options.D: Discarding digital backups immediately to save storage space

explanation: You nailed it! Deleting your backups is a huge risk that can lead to permanent data loss—definitely something we want to avoid! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T20#GNS224_U1_T20_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a research instrument in nursing studies?

options.A: To write the final research report
options.B: To treat patient clinical symptoms
options.C: To fund the research project
options.D: To collect and measure study data

explanation: A research instrument acts as the tool used to gather and measure information needed to answer a research question. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h1)

question: Why are research instruments compared to clinical tools like a thermometer?

options.A: They both need precision to capture accurate information.
options.B: They are both disposable after a single patient use.
options.C: They are both used exclusively in hospital emergency rooms.
options.D: They both require electricity to function properly.

explanation: Just as a thermometer must be accurate to measure body heat, a research instrument must be precise to capture true data. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h1)

question: What does a valid research instrument do?

options.A: Measures what it is supposed to measure
options.B: Costs very little money to print out
options.C: Takes less than five minutes to finish
options.D: Gives the exact same results every time

explanation: Validity is all about accuracy, meaning the tool actually captures the specific concept being studied. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h2)

question: A nurse uses a pain scale that somehow measures patient hunger instead of pain. Which quality is this tool lacking?

options.A: Reliability
options.B: Length
options.C: Practicality
options.D: Validity

explanation: When an instrument measures the wrong concept, it lacks validity because it is not capturing what it claims to measure. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h2)

question: Which instrument is best for capturing deep, personal stories from patients about chronic illness?

options.A: Interview guide
options.B: Simple questionnaire
options.C: Blood pressure cuff
options.D: Checklist of bedside actions

explanation: Interview guides allow researchers to ask open-ended questions and explore personal experiences in detail. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h3)

question: A researcher wants to record the exact physical behaviors of nurses during a sterile dressing change. Which instrument should they use?

options.A: Observational checklist
options.B: Structured interview guide
options.C: Patient satisfaction survey
options.D: Biographical questionnaire

explanation: Observational checklists are ideal for watching and recording specific actions as they happen in real time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h3)

question: What is a double-barreled question in a research instrument?

options.A: A question that has more than ten possible answers
options.B: A question written in two different languages
options.C: A question that is asked twice during an interview
options.D: A question that asks about two different things at once

explanation: Double-barreled questions confuse respondents because they combine multiple ideas into a single query. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h4)

question: Why is it important to test draft survey questions on a small group before the main study?

options.A: To force participants to agree with the researcher
options.B: To finish the research project much faster
options.C: To catch hidden mistakes and confusing wording
options.D: To make the final paper look longer and better

explanation: Pilot testing helps identify confusing questions and errors before you spend time and resources on the full study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h4)

question: Why might a nurse researcher choose an observational checklist instead of a patient questionnaire?

options.A: Patients prefer being watched over writing answers
options.B: What people say they do can differ from their actual actions
options.C: Observational checklists are much cheaper to print
options.D: Questionnaires cannot be used in a hospital setting

explanation: Direct observation captures real behavior, avoiding the bias or forgetfulness that comes with self-reporting. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h5)

question: What is a major benefit of using physiological measures like a blood pressure machine in research?

options.A: They eliminate the need for any human researchers
options.B: They cost nothing to purchase and maintain
options.C: They take the place of nursing clinical judgment
options.D: They provide objective data that cannot be falsified by memory

explanation: Physiological tools measure physical states directly, providing reliable, objective data without relying on patient memory. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h5)

question: Which type of validity involves checking if a new tool compares well with an established gold standard?

options.A: Surface validity
options.B: Criterion validity
options.C: Face validity
options.D: Content validity

explanation: Criterion validity is established when a new instrument scores similarly to a trusted, proven gold-standard tool. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h6)

question: A panel of senior nurses reviews a new questionnaire to see if it covers every aspect of post-operative care. What are they testing?

options.A: Content validity
options.B: Physical durability
options.C: Data entry speed
options.D: Test-retest reliability

explanation: Content validity ensures that the tool covers all important dimensions of the subject being studied. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h6)

question: What statistical value is commonly used to measure the internal consistency of a questionnaire?

options.A: Cronbach's alpha
options.B: Celsius scale
options.C: Body mass index
options.D: P-value index

explanation: Cronbach's alpha is the standard statistical test used to check if items within a scale relate well to one another. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h7)

question: Two clinical supervisors watch the same nursing student perform a procedure and grade them using the same checklist. What are they checking?

options.A: Test-retest validity
options.B: Content consistency
options.C: Inter-rater reliability
options.D: Patient satisfaction

explanation: Inter-rater reliability checks whether different observers get similar scores when using the exact same tool. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h7)

question: Why must researchers follow a standardized procedure during data collection?

options.A: To make the research process take longer
options.B: To avoid getting permission from the hospital
options.C: To ensure patients pay for their participation
options.D: To prevent outside disturbances from ruining results

explanation: Standardized procedures ensure every participant has the same experience, keeping data collection consistent and reliable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h8)

question: What is the primary reason for keeping completed research questionnaires in a locked cabinet?

options.A: To ensure the forms do not get misplaced by staff
options.B: To make sure nobody steals the paper pens
options.C: To protect patient confidentiality and privacy
options.D: To comply with hospital interior design rules

explanation: Securing completed research documents is an ethical duty to protect participants' private health information. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h8)

question: What is the main purpose of a questionnaire in nursing research?

options.A: To perform direct physical examinations on patients
options.B: To prescribe medication adjustments based on lab work
options.C: To replace the need for informed consent in a study
options.D: To gather structured data directly from participants

explanation: A questionnaire is specifically designed as a written tool to collect standardized information straight from respondents. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h1)

question: Why do researchers use the exact same questions and words for everyone taking a survey?

options.A: It prevents participants from feeling confused by long medical terms
options.B: It guarantees that every participant will finish the survey faster
options.C: It allows the nurse researcher to change the topic mid-interview
options.D: It ensures all answers can be fairly compared across the group

explanation: Using identical wording means any differences in the responses are due to actual differences between people, not because a question was asked differently. Keep pushing forward! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h1)

question: What kind of survey question gives people a fixed list of choices to pick from?

options.A: Unstructured item
options.B: Open-ended item
options.C: Closed-ended item
options.D: Narrative item

explanation: Closed-ended items restrict answers to predefined options, which makes counting and analyzing the responses much easier for your research project. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h2)

question: A nurse wants to measure patient satisfaction using options from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. Which format should she use?

options.A: Likert scale
options.B: Open-ended essay
options.C: Dichotomous checklist
options.D: Biographical interview

explanation: A Likert scale is designed specifically to measure attitudes and agreement levels across a multi-point scale. Great job learning the research tools! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h2)

question: What is a 'double-barreled' question in a research survey?

options.A: A question placed at the very end of a long research tool
options.B: A single question that mistakenly asks about two different things
options.C: A question that offers more than five possible answer choices
options.D: A survey item written in two different languages at once

explanation: Double-barreled questions confuse respondents because they cannot give separate answers to two different ideas packed into one sentence. You'll master questionnaire design in no time! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h3)

question: Why is it best to put easy, general questions at the very beginning of a survey?

options.A: To trick the participant into answering difficult items quickly
options.B: To ensure the statistical software can read the demographic data
options.C: To shorten the total amount of time needed for data collection
options.D: To help the participant feel comfortable and build trust

explanation: Starting with gentle, straightforward questions eases anxiety and encourages people to complete the rest of the questionnaire. Brilliant thinking! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h3)

question: In research, what does the 'validity' of a questionnaire mean?

options.A: Whether the tool can be completed in under ten minutes
options.B: Whether the tool measures what it is intended to measure
options.C: Whether the tool was printed on approved institutional paper
options.D: Whether the tool gives the exact same scores on repeat testing

explanation: Validity checks if your questions are truly capturing the specific concept or variable you set out to study. You're building solid clinical research skills! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h4)

question: What does it mean if a research questionnaire is described as 'reliable'?

options.A: It successfully measures complex human emotions accurately
options.B: It has been approved by the hospital ethics committee
options.C: It gives consistent results when used repeatedly over time
options.D: It is completely free from any potential ethical violations

explanation: Reliability is all about consistency. A reliable tool yields similar scores when conditions remain stable. Keep up the great work! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h4)

question: What is a major downside of using online questionnaires for hospital patients?

options.A: They prevent researchers from collecting any numerical data
options.B: They force patients to answer every question before submitting
options.C: They always cost significantly more than printed paper surveys
options.D: They may exclude patients who lack internet access or devices

explanation: The digital divide means older or lower-income patients might not have the technology required to complete online forms. Excellent real-world nursing perspective! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h5)

question: Which way of giving out a survey lets a nurse directly clarify confusing items for the respondent?

options.A: Anonymous drop-off boxes
options.B: Face-to-face administration
options.C: Unmonitored online web links
options.D: Standard postal mail surveys

explanation: When you are present during survey administration, you can immediately explain what a question means if the participant looks confused. Spot on! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h5)

question: What is the main reason for running a 'pilot test' on a questionnaire before a big study?

options.A: To identify and fix problems before the main study begins
options.B: To permanently replace the need for an ethics review
options.C: To publish the final research results ahead of schedule
options.D: To recruit participants who will drop out of the study

explanation: Pilot testing lets researchers spot unclear wording or formatting errors on a small group before spending resources on the full study. Smart thinking! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h6)

question: Who should ideally test out a draft questionnaire in the pre-testing phase?

options.A: Only senior professors who have published many research papers
options.B: Patients who have already completed the final main survey
options.C: Hospital accountants who manage the research funding budget
options.D: People who share similar characteristics with your target study group
